metadata.summary: This guideline addresses prostate cancer early detection in people with a prostate who choose to participate after discussing potential benefits and harms. It covers risk assessment, PSA-based testing, decisions about further evaluation and biopsy, biopsy methods, and management of biopsy findings. It aims to identify clinically significant cancer while limiting unnecessary procedures and detection of indolent disease; prostate cancer treatment recommendations are outside its scope.

target_population: Informed, healthy individuals with a prostate who choose to participate in early detection
Individuals at average risk aged 45–75 years
Individuals at high risk aged 40–75 years
Select very healthy individuals aged >75 years

toxicities.incidence: In U.S. hospitals from 2009 to 2016, the 30-day risk of invasive Escherichia coli infection was 5.0 per 1000 patients; this figure is not identified as a prostate-biopsy-specific rate. Studies reported that up to 78% of post-biopsy infections were resistant to fluoroquinolone.
prevention: Antimicrobial prophylaxis is generally used for transrectal biopsy.
Apply stringent criteria when deciding whether biopsy is needed.
A transperineal approach may lower sepsis risk and antibiotic use compared with a transrectal approach, although the evidence conflicts.

toxicities.event: Bleeding and other noninfectious complications of prostate biopsy

toxicities.incidence: Up to 90% of individuals undergoing prostate biopsy reported some discomfort during the procedure.
prevention: Minor anesthetic techniques should be considered for all patients, particularly when extended templates or saturation techniques are used.

Topical lidocaine gel and an injectable nerve block have each reduced discomfort; topical lidocaine was more effective during probe insertion, whereas periprostatic injection reduced pain during the biopsy.

Small trials suggested greater pain relief with a lidocaine suppository plus periprostatic nerve block than with either alone, and identified lidocaine plus pelvic plexus block as the most effective approach studied in another trial.

A randomized trial in 216 patients undergoing TRUS-guided transperineal biopsy found less pain during biopsy with peri-prostatic nerve block, subcutaneous perineal anesthesia, and intrarectal lidocaine gel than with total intravenous anesthesia.

Deep sedation or general anesthesia may be advantageous for individuals with anal strictures, those who cannot readily tolerate biopsy under local anesthesia, or those inadequately blocked by periprostatic injection.

toxicities.event: Potential serious adverse effects of fluoroquinolone
recognition: Potentially disabling or permanent effects involving tendons, muscles, joints, nerves, or the central nervous system

toxicities.event: Harms of prostate cancer early detection
recognition: Overdetection of disease that would not have caused a problem if left unidentified
Potential overtreatment of low-risk disease without clinical benefit
False-positive PSA results that can cause anxiety and lead to unnecessary biopsies, costs, and complications
prevention: Discuss the benefits and harms before participation in early detection, and account for patient preferences.
Use risk-informed evaluation to limit unnecessary biopsies and detection of indolent disease.
The guidelines favor selective rather than uniform treatment after cancer detection.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Antimicrobial prophylaxis is generally used with transrectal biopsy to prevent infection and reduce the need for antibiotics afterward. The American Urological Association (AUA) states that fluoroquinolone prophylaxis should be considered in some centers and clinical circumstances; its other recommended options are 1st/2nd generation cephalosporin with or without aminoglycoside, or 3rd generation cephalosporin.
Pre-biopsy rectal culture to guide selective antibiotic prophylaxis is described as a proposed infection-prevention strategy.
Prophylaxis with two antibiotics is described as a proposed strategy for patients at elevated infection risk.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients at elevated risk for infection undergoing prostate biopsy

infection_management.prevention: Antimicrobial prophylaxis is generally used for transrectal biopsy. Restrictive biopsy criteria and a transperineal approach are discussed as ways to limit infection risk, although comparative evidence for the latter conflicts.
infection_management.management: The guideline states that infections resistant to fluoroquinolone respond to cephalosporins, without specifying a treatment protocol.

therapies_index.name: PSA testing
approved_indications: Early detection of prostate cancer in informed, healthy individuals with a prostate who elect to participate in an early detection program.
therapies_index.administration: Baseline testing is offered at ages 45 to 75 years for individuals at average risk and at ages 40 to 75 years for those at elevated risk. Subsequent intervals depend on risk and PSA results.
key_toxicities: False-positive results may cause anxiety and lead to unnecessary biopsies.
Screening may detect indolent cancers and contribute to overdiagnosis and overtreatment.
monitoring: Confirm an elevated result with repeat testing, particularly when it is near a threshold for further evaluation.
Use the PSA result and individual risk to determine subsequent testing intervals.

therapies_index.name: digital rectal examination (DRE)
approved_indications: Optional complement to baseline serum PSA testing.
Assessment of an elevated PSA and decisions about further evaluation or biopsy.

therapies_index.name: Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI)
approved_indications: Evaluation before prostate biopsy, if available, to inform the biopsy decision and locate suspicious regions.
Consideration after a negative biopsy if concern for cancer persists and high-quality imaging has not already been performed.
therapies_index.administration: Perform before biopsy when available.
monitoring: A negative result does not rule out clinically significant cancer; consider PSA density or other biomarkers when deciding whether biopsy remains necessary.

therapies_index.name: image-guided biopsy
approved_indications: Prostate sampling when suspicion of clinically significant cancer is high.
therapies_index.administration: A transrectal or transperineal approach may be used; targeting of lesions identified on pre-biopsy MRI is preferred when available.
key_toxicities: Infection, bleeding, hematuria, vasovagal episodes, fever, hematospermia, dysuria and procedural discomfort.

therapies_index.name: transrectal biopsy
approved_indications: Prostate biopsy through a transrectal approach.
therapies_index.administration: Antimicrobial prophylaxis is generally used.
key_toxicities: Post-biopsy infection, including infection caused by antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli.

therapies_index.name: transperineal biopsy
approved_indications: Prostate biopsy through a transperineal approach.
key_toxicities: Extensive perineal template sampling may increase urinary retention.

therapies_index.name: systematic biopsy
approved_indications: Sampling alongside MRI-targeted biopsy, particularly at initial biopsy, to improve detection and support risk stratification.
therapies_index.administration: When systematic sampling is performed, an extended pattern with at least 12 cores is recommended.

therapies_index.name: MRI-targeted biopsy
approved_indications: Targeted sampling of regions identified on MRI at initial biopsy or when suspicion persists after a negative biopsy.
therapies_index.administration: Use MRI targeting when the capability is available; combining targeted and systematic sampling is preferred at initial biopsy.

therapies_index.name: MRI/ultrasound fusion
approved_indications: Image-guided targeting during prostate biopsy, including assessment after a negative biopsy when cancer remains a concern.
therapies_index.administration: Target biopsy sites by combining MRI and ultrasound images.

therapies_index.name: cognitive or visual targeting
approved_indications: Targeted prostate biopsy of a lesion seen on MRI.
therapies_index.administration: Guide ultrasound-based sampling using the MRI image as a visual reference.

therapies_index.name: direct in-bore magnetic resonance (MR)-guided biopsy
approved_indications: MRI-targeted prostate biopsy.
therapies_index.administration: An interventional radiologist performs the biopsy while the patient is in the scanner.

therapies_index.name: transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) biopsy
approved_indications: Image-guided prostate sampling.

therapies_index.name: saturation biopsy
approved_indications: An approach studied for further sampling after a negative prostate biopsy; the panel does not recommend it for all such individuals.
therapies_index.administration: Collect cores systematically every few millimeters throughout the prostate, using a transrectal or transperineal approach.

therapies_index.name: anteriorly directed biopsy
approved_indications: Possible addition to an extended repeat-biopsy protocol when PSA remains elevated; routine use is not supported.

therapies_index.name: repeat prostate biopsy
approved_indications: Further assessment when concern for cancer remains after a negative biopsy.
Investigation for invasive carcinoma after a biopsy showing AIP without invasive carcinoma.
therapies_index.administration: For AIP without invasive carcinoma, use both MRI targeting and systematic sampling. For atypia suspicious for cancer, consider repeat sampling in 12–24 months with relatively greater sampling of the atypical site.

therapies_index.name: active surveillance
approved_indications: Management of appropriate patients diagnosed with prostate cancer instead of immediate treatment, as addressed in the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer.

therapies_index.name: observation
approved_indications: Management of appropriate patients diagnosed with prostate cancer, as addressed in the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer.

therapies_index.name: genetic testing
approved_indications: Assessment of patients with a suspicious family history of cancer or appropriate hereditary cancer risk criteria.

therapies_index.name: genetic counseling
approved_indications: Referral when a cancer susceptibility gene is known or suspected, or when hereditary risk assessment criteria are met.

therapies_index.name: %fPSA
approved_indications: FDA-approved for early prostate cancer detection in individuals aged ≥50 years with a non-suspicious DRE and PSA between 4 and 10 ng/mL.
An option before initial biopsy and after a negative biopsy.
therapies_index.administration: Express free PSA as a proportion of total PSA.

therapies_index.name: PSA density
approved_indications: An aid to biopsy decisions in biopsy-naïve patients with elevated PSA or in those with a negative mpMRI.
therapies_index.administration: Requires image-based prostate volume measurement; calculate PSA in ng/mL divided by prostate volume in cc.

therapies_index.name: PCA3
approved_indications: FDA-approved to help determine, alongside other factors, whether repeat biopsy is needed in individuals aged ≥50 years with one or more prior negative prostate biopsies.
An option after a negative biopsy; the panel does not consider it appropriate for initial-biopsy decisions.
therapies_index.administration: The assay uses urine collected after DRE.

therapies_index.name: Prostate Health Index (PHI)
approved_indications: FDA-approved for individuals with serum PSA between 4 and 10 ng/mL.
An option before initial biopsy and after a negative biopsy.

therapies_index.name: 4Kscore
approved_indications: Consideration before biopsy or after a negative biopsy when risk of clinically significant prostate cancer remains elevated.
therapies_index.administration: The assessment also incorporates age, DRE findings and prior biopsy status.
monitoring: Discuss the result with the patient when deciding whether to biopsy; an optimal cutoff has not been established.

therapies_index.name: ConfirmMDx
therapies_index.mechanism: Assesses promoter hypermethylation of GSTP1, APC, and RASSF1 in prostate biopsy tissue.
approved_indications: An option when considering repeat biopsy after a negative result.
therapies_index.administration: Uses tissue from prostate biopsy cores.

therapies_index.name: ExoDx Prostate (IntelliScore)
therapies_index.mechanism: Assesses urinary exosome expression of PCA3 and ERG RNA relative to SPDEF.
approved_indications: An option when considering initial or repeat prostate biopsy.
therapies_index.administration: Urine-based assay.

therapies_index.name: SelectMDx
therapies_index.mechanism: Measures DLX1 and HOXC6 expression using KLK3 as an internal reference.
approved_indications: Consideration before biopsy in individuals who have not previously undergone biopsy.
therapies_index.administration: Uses urine collected after DRE.

therapies_index.name: IsoPSA
therapies_index.mechanism: Partitions and detects blood PSA isoforms using an aqueous 2-phase system.
approved_indications: Consideration before biopsy or after a negative biopsy when concern for clinically significant prostate cancer persists.
therapies_index.administration: Blood-based assay.

therapies_index.name: MyProstateScore (MPS)
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines total serum PSA with urinary PCA3 and TMPRSS2:ERG expression.
approved_indications: Consideration before biopsy or after a negative biopsy when risk of clinically significant prostate cancer remains elevated.
therapies_index.administration: Uses serum and urine collected after DRE.

therapies_index.name: MiR Sentinel Prostate Cancer Test
therapies_index.mechanism: Interrogates small noncoding RNAs isolated from urinary exosomes.
therapies_index.administration: Urine-based assay.

therapies_index.name: Stockholm3
therapies_index.administration: The model combines clinical variables, blood biomarkers, a genetic score, prostate volume and DRE findings.

therapies_index.name: finasteride
approved_indications: Treatment of lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic hyperplasia.
Treatment of male-pattern baldness at 1 mg/day.
therapies_index.administration: The guide specifies 1 mg/day for male-pattern baldness.
monitoring: Account for treatment and its duration when interpreting PSA because PSA may fall; a substantial failure to fall or a confirmed rise from the post-treatment nadir may warrant attention.

therapies_index.name: dutasteride
approved_indications: Treatment of lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic hyperplasia.
monitoring: Account for treatment and its duration when interpreting PSA because PSA may fall; a substantial failure to fall or a confirmed rise from the post-treatment nadir may warrant attention.

therapies_index.name: tamsulosin
approved_indications: Treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia.

therapies_index.name: ketoconazole
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits androgen synthesis and can lower PSA.
approved_indications: Treatment of fungal conditions.
monitoring: Record recent use when assessing PSA results.

therapies_index.name: antimicrobial prophylaxis
approved_indications: Generally used with transrectal prostate biopsy to prevent infection and reduce the need for antibiotics after the procedure.
therapies_index.administration: The guide also describes proposed approaches using a pre-biopsy rectal culture to direct prophylaxis or augmenting prophylaxis with two antibiotics for patients at elevated infection risk.

therapies_index.name: fluoroquinolone
approved_indications: Prophylaxis for transrectal biopsy in some centers and clinical circumstances, as acknowledged by the AUA.
key_toxicities: Drug-class warnings include potentially disabling and permanent effects involving tendons, muscles, joints, nerves and the central nervous system; aortic rupture or tears; serious hypoglycemia; and mental health effects.

therapies_index.name: 1st/2nd generation cephalosporin
approved_indications: An AUA-listed antimicrobial prophylaxis option for transrectal biopsy, with or without aminoglycoside.

therapies_index.name: 3rd generation cephalosporin
approved_indications: An AUA-listed antimicrobial prophylaxis option for transrectal biopsy.

therapies_index.name: aminoglycoside
approved_indications: An optional addition to 1st/2nd generation cephalosporin for transrectal-biopsy prophylaxis in the AUA-listed options.

therapies_index.name: lidocaine
approved_indications: Reduction of discomfort during prostate biopsy.
therapies_index.administration: The guide describes topical gel, suppository and injectable anesthetic approaches.

therapies_index.name: periprostatic nerve block
approved_indications: Reduction of pain during prostate biopsy.
therapies_index.administration: The guide also discusses its use with a lidocaine suppository.

therapies_index.name: pelvic plexus block
approved_indications: Reduction of biopsy-related pain when combined with lidocaine in a cited small trial.

therapies_index.name: subcutaneous perineal anesthesia
approved_indications: Anesthesia for TRUS-guided transperineal prostate biopsy in a cited trial.

therapies_index.name: deep sedation
approved_indications: A potentially advantageous approach when local anesthesia is poorly tolerated or inadequate, or in circumstances such as anal strictures.

therapies_index.name: general anesthesia
approved_indications: A potentially advantageous approach when local anesthesia is poorly tolerated or inadequate, or in circumstances such as anal strictures.

artifacts.title: Baseline Evaluation, Risk Assessment, and Early Detection Evaluation
artifacts.description: Step 1: Obtain history and physical examination, including family cancer history; personal or family history of high-risk germline mutations; previous prostate disease, PSA testing, examinations, and biopsies; Black/African American identity; medications; and environmental exposure. Discuss the potential benefits and risks of early detection, obtain baseline PSA, and consider baseline DRE. Step 2: For patients at high risk aged 40–75 y, including Black/African American individuals, people with relevant germline mutations, and those with concerning family or personal history, proceed with early-detection evaluation. For average-risk patients, the corresponding age range is 45–75 y. Consider evaluation after age >75 y only in selected patients (category 2B); otherwise, do not screen. Step 3: For average-risk patients with PSA <1 ng/mL and normal DRE if performed, repeat testing at 2- to 4-year intervals. For high-risk patients with PSA ≤3 ng/mL or average-risk patients with PSA 1–3 ng/mL, with normal DRE if performed, repeat testing at 1 to 2-year intervals; consider further evaluation in younger patients. Step 4: If PSA >3 ng/mL and/or DRE is very suspicious, proceed to further evaluation and consideration of biopsy. Step 5: In selected patients aged >75 y, if PSA <4 ng/mL, DRE is normal if performed, and there is no other biopsy indication, repeat testing at 1 to 3-year intervals or consider stopping screening when clinically appropriate. If PSA ≥4 ng/mL or DRE is very suspicious, proceed to further evaluation.
artifacts.summary: The flowchart connects baseline risk assessment and PSA testing to age-, risk-, and result-dependent screening intervals or further evaluation. Screening after age >75 y is limited to selected patients.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It directs when to start evaluation, when to repeat testing, and when findings warrant a biopsy-oriented assessment.

artifacts.title: Further Evaluation and Indications for Biopsy
artifacts.source_heading: FURTHER EVALUATION AND INDICATIONS FOR BIOPSY (PROSD-3)
artifacts.description: Step 1: Repeat PSA, perform DRE if it was not part of the initial assessment, and assess for benign disease. Step 2: Obtain mpMRI (category 1) when available and consider biomarkers that increase screening specificity. Step 3: If suspicion for clinically significant cancer is high, proceed with image-guided biopsy by a transrectal or transperineal route, preferably with MRI targeting; biopsy without MRI targeting is also shown. Step 4: If suspicion is low, follow up with PSA and DRE in 6–12 mo. A negative MRI does not rule out cancer; biomarker findings and PSA density can inform whether biopsy is avoided. Patients with a persistent, substantial PSA increase, including those with greater PSA density, should be encouraged to undergo biopsy even when MRI is normal.
artifacts.summary: The flowchart moves from confirmatory assessment and optional risk-refining tests to biopsy or PSA/DRE follow-up according to clinical suspicion. It includes the limitations of a negative MRI.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It supports biopsy decisions while accounting for benign causes of PSA elevation and the possibility of clinically significant cancer despite a normal MRI.

artifacts.title: Management of Biopsy Results
artifacts.description: Step 1: If biopsy identifies cancer, refer to NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer. Step 2: If IDC is found without invasive carcinoma, consider definitive treatment; otherwise, evaluate carefully and strongly consider another MRI-targeted biopsy to seek invasive cancer. Step 3: If AIP is found without invasive carcinoma, repeat biopsy using MRI targeting and systematic sampling to seek invasive carcinoma. Step 4: For atypia suspicious for cancer, high-grade PIN, or benign findings, determine whether a previous high-quality mpMRI was performed. Without one, consider biomarkers that improve screening specificity and/or mpMRI. For atypia, consider another biopsy in 12–24 months with relatively greater sampling of the atypical area. With a previous high-quality mpMRI, perform PSA and DRE at 12- to 24-month intervals and consider specificity-improving biomarkers. Step 5: If suspicion of cancer remains high, repeat prostate biopsy using refined techniques.
artifacts.summary: The flowchart assigns distinct next steps to cancer, IDC, AIP, atypia, high-grade PIN, and benign biopsy findings. Prior high-quality mpMRI and ongoing cancer suspicion determine subsequent testing or repeat biopsy.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It distinguishes findings that warrant prompt investigation for invasive cancer from findings managed with surveillance and selective repeat biopsy.

artifacts.title: General Considerations for Early Detection
artifacts.source_heading: Summary of NCCN Recommendations for Early Detection — General Considerations

rows: Retain a full medical history and physical examination when assessing early detection.
Account for overall health, comorbidities, life expectancy, and patient preferences.
Assess family history, inherited mutations, and African ancestry before deciding when to begin.

Explain that early prostate cancer has no identifiable symptoms, while advanced disease can cause urinary obstruction, prostatic bleeding, hematospermia, or bone pain; distinguish this from symptoms associated with benign enlargement.
Review previous DRE, PSA, PSA derivatives, and prostate biopsies.
Discuss potential benefits and harms, including detection of low-risk cancers that may be managed by active surveillance rather than immediate treatment.
Offer baseline PSA testing to informed, healthy average-risk individuals aged 45 to 75 years; DRE may complement it, and an elevated PSA should be confirmed with repeat testing.
Offer baseline PSA testing at ages 40 to 75 years to informed, healthy individuals with African ancestry, relevant germline mutations, and/or suspicious family history.

For average-risk individuals <75 years with PSA below 1 ng/mL, test every 2 to 4 years; with PSA 1 to 3 ng/mL, test at 1- to 2-year intervals. For higher-risk individuals with PSA ≤3 ng/mL, test at 1 to 2-year intervals.
Perform mpMRI before biopsy if available; consider specified biomarkers when additional biopsy specificity is desired.
Base biopsy decisions on clinical factors, patient preferences, and mpMRI and/or biomarker results, rather than a PSA threshold alone.
For high suspicion of clinically significant cancer, use image-guided transrectal or transperineal biopsy and routinely use MRI targeting where available.
Consider PSA testing after age >75 years only cautiously in very healthy patients (category 2B); discourage testing when age and/or comorbidity make benefit from diagnosis unlikely.

recommendations.statement: Discuss the potential benefits and harms of prostate cancer early detection before an individual chooses to participate.
recommendations.context: An early detection program is intended for informed individuals with a prostate who elect to participate; the panel does not support unselected, uninformed population-based screening.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The discussion should address the possibility of finding aggressive cancer alongside unnecessary biopsies, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment.

recommendations.statement: Before planning early detection, obtain a history and physical that addresses family cancer history, personal or familial high-risk germline mutations, prior prostate disease and early detection results, Black/African American identity, medications, and environmental exposures.
recommendations.context: Prior results include PSA and/or its isoforms, examinations, and biopsies.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: These factors inform the individual's risk and the timing of early detection.

recommendations.statement: Offer baseline PSA testing to healthy, informed individuals at average risk who are aged 45–75 y; a baseline DRE may be considered in addition.
recommendations.context: The offer follows a discussion of the risks and benefits of early detection.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The panel cites randomized evidence supporting PSA-based early detection while recognizing the harms of overdetection.
recommendations.source_heading: Summary of NCCN Recommendations for Early Detection

recommendations.statement: Offer baseline PSA testing to healthy, informed individuals at elevated risk who are aged 40–75 y.
recommendations.context: The elevated-risk groups include Black/African American individuals, people with germline mutations that increase prostate cancer risk, and those with a concerning family or personal history.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: These groups have an increased risk of developing prostate cancer.
recommendations.source_heading: Summary of NCCN Recommendations for Early Detection

recommendations.statement: Recommend prostate cancer early detection beginning at age 40 years for BRCA2 carriers.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: BRCA2 carriers have increased prostate cancer risk, including risk of earlier-onset or potentially lethal disease.
recommendations.source_heading: Recommendations for Early Detection in Populations with Elevated Risk

recommendations.statement: Individuals with other germline mutations may reasonably consider shared decision-making about PSA screening at age 40 years and annual rather than every-other-year screening.
recommendations.context: This applies to germline mutations associated with increased prostate cancer risk other than BRCA2.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The panel notes that available data do not definitively establish the best early detection strategy for elevated-risk groups.
recommendations.source_heading: Recommendations for Early Detection in Populations with Elevated Risk

recommendations.statement: Individuals with a suspicious family cancer history should begin shared decision-making about PSA screening at age 40 years.
recommendations.context: The guideline's family history criteria include specified cancers in first- or second-degree relatives and affected relatives' ages or numbers.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: A concerning family history can inform when to begin discussing early detection.
recommendations.source_heading: Recommendations for Early Detection in Populations with Elevated Risk

recommendations.statement: Black/African American individuals should consider beginning shared decision-making about PSA screening at age 40 years and consider annual rather than every-other-year screening.
recommendations.context: Earlier screening may increase overdiagnosis; current evidence does not show that starting earlier reduces morbidity or mortality compared with starting at age 45.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The panel identifies a higher incidence, greater mortality, and earlier diagnosis of prostate cancer in this population, while acknowledging uncertainty about the benefit of earlier screening.
recommendations.source_heading: Recommendations for Early Detection in Populations with Elevated Risk

recommendations.statement: Recommend shared decision-making about the timing and frequency of PSA testing when genetic testing identifies no germline mutation in a prostate cancer risk gene but the family history remains concerning.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: A concerning family history remains relevant to risk assessment despite a negative genetic test.

recommendations.statement: Arrange genetic testing for patients with a suspicious family history.
recommendations.context: The guideline identifies family and personal cancer histories that warrant hereditary risk assessment.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: An inherited predisposition may affect prostate cancer risk and early detection decisions.

recommendations.statement: Ask about known personal or familial germline mutations associated with increased cancer risk, and refer individuals with a known or suspected cancer susceptibility gene to a cancer genetics professional.
recommendations.context: Use mutation status when discussing prostate cancer early detection.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Individuals may not know that their germline mutation increases prostate cancer risk.

recommendations.statement: Refer patients who meet hereditary risk assessment criteria in the NCCN Guidelines for Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment: Breast, Ovarian, and Pancreatic or the NCCN Guidelines for Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment: Colorectal for genetic counseling and testing as appropriate.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus

recommendations.statement: Inform patients exposed to Agent Orange that this exposure may be associated with increased risk of high-grade prostate cancer.
recommendations.context: The guideline mentions Vietnam War veterans as an example of an exposed group.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The association is presented as possible, not established.
recommendations.source_heading: Screening in Populations with Elevated Risk

recommendations.statement: Use serum PSA for early detection; do not use DRE as the sole early detection test.
recommendations.context: DRE may be considered as a complementary baseline examination and is most useful when PSA is elevated.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: DRE alone misses clinically significant cancers and has poor positive predictive value.

recommendations.statement: Confirm an elevated PSA with repeat testing.
recommendations.context: Repeating the test is particularly important when the result is close to a threshold that prompts further evaluation.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: An initially elevated result can return to the normal range on repeat testing.
recommendations.source_heading: Summary of NCCN Recommendations for Early Detection

recommendations.statement: For individuals at average risk with PSA <1 ng/mL and a normal DRE if performed, repeat testing at 2- to 4-year intervals.
recommendations.context: This pathway applies to the early detection age group through 75 y.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Lower PSA values are associated with a lower subsequent risk, supporting a longer testing interval.

recommendations.statement: For individuals at high risk with PSA ≤3 ng/mL and a normal DRE if performed, repeat testing at 1 to 2-year intervals.
recommendations.context: For younger individuals, further evaluation may also be considered.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The recommended interval reflects the individual's elevated risk.

recommendations.statement: For individuals at average risk with PSA 1–3 ng/mL and a normal DRE if performed, repeat testing at 1 to 2-year intervals.
recommendations.context: For younger individuals, further evaluation may also be considered.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: PSA level and individual risk inform the testing interval.

recommendations.statement: Consider further evaluation for individuals whose PSA exceeds the median for their age group, even when it does not exceed >3 ng/mL.
recommendations.context: The guideline particularly raises further evaluation as an option for younger patients.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Prostate cancer risk rises as PSA increases above the age-group median.

recommendations.statement: Refer individuals with PSA >3 ng/mL and/or a DRE that is very suspicious for cancer for further evaluation concerning biopsy.
recommendations.context: A DRE highly suspicious for cancer warrants evaluation regardless of the PSA result.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: PSA and a highly suspicious examination can indicate clinically significant disease.

recommendations.statement: Do not offer PSA testing to individuals with a life expectancy of less than 10 years.
recommendations.context: Health status, comorbidities, life expectancy, and patient preferences should guide early detection decisions.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The panel considers these individuals unlikely to benefit from a prostate cancer diagnosis.
recommendations.source_heading: Age at Which to Discontinue Testing

recommendations.statement: Consider continued PSA-based early detection after age 75 years only for selected, very healthy individuals with little or no comorbidity.
recommendations.context: Particular consideration may apply to those never tested with PSA or whose PSA is rising; widespread testing in this age group is not recommended.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Selective testing could detect aggressive cancers, whereas widespread testing would substantially increase overdetection.
recommendations.source_heading: Age at Which to Discontinue Testing

recommendations.statement: For selected individuals >75 years who continue early detection and have PSA <4 ng/mL, a normal DRE if performed, and no other indication for biopsy, repeat testing at 1 to 3-year intervals or consider stopping screening when clinically appropriate.
recommendations.context: Continued testing is limited to very healthy individuals with little or no comorbidity.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Screening decisions in this age group require a balance between identifying aggressive disease and avoiding overdetection.
recommendations.source_heading: Age at Which to Discontinue Testing

recommendations.statement: Further evaluate individuals >75 years who continue early detection if PSA is ≥4 ng/mL or DRE is very suspicious for cancer.
recommendations.context: The higher PSA threshold applies to those who choose to continue screening beyond age 75 years.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The decision to investigate a possible aggressive cancer must be weighed against harms of testing in this age group.
recommendations.source_heading: Age at Which to Discontinue Testing

recommendations.statement: For an individual with PSA >3 ng/mL, repeat PSA, perform DRE if it was not part of the initial assessment, and evaluate for benign disease before deciding on biopsy or additional testing.
recommendations.context: The subsequent decision may incorporate biomarkers and/or mpMRI.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: These findings help determine whether biopsy is warranted.

recommendations.statement: Strongly recommend mpMRI before prostate biopsy when it is available.
recommendations.context: Use the examination to guide the biopsy decision and identify potentially cancer-bearing regions.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Pre-biopsy imaging can help reduce unnecessary biopsies and identify clinically significant disease, although a negative examination does not rule out cancer.

recommendations.statement: Consider biomarkers that improve screening specificity before biopsy when additional risk clarification is desired.
recommendations.context: Options discussed for the pre-biopsy setting include %fPSA, 4Kscore, SelectMDx, ExoDx Prostate, PHI, MPS, and IsoPSA, particularly for individuals with PSA >3 ng/mL who seek greater specificity.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The tests may help reduce unnecessary biopsies, but their optimal combination with mpMRI is uncertain.
recommendations.source_heading: Summary of NCCN Recommendations for Early Detection

recommendations.statement: Consider biomarkers and/or PSA density when deciding whether biopsy can be avoided after a negative mpMRI.
recommendations.context: A negative MRI does not exclude prostate cancer; biopsy should still be considered when other indicators suggest high risk.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Clinically significant cancers can be missed on mpMRI.
recommendations.source_heading: Further Evaluation and Indications for Biopsy

recommendations.statement: Consider PSA density when deciding whether a biopsy is needed in a biopsy-naïve individual with elevated PSA.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: PSA density may help distinguish PSA elevation associated with a large prostate from elevation associated with cancer.

recommendations.statement: Do not determine the need for biopsy from a PSA threshold alone; incorporate clinical variables, patient preferences, and available mpMRI and/or biomarker findings.
recommendations.context: The guideline identifies age, family history, PSA kinetics, ancestry, and health status among the relevant variables.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Individual cancer risk cannot be captured by one PSA cut-point.
recommendations.source_heading: Summary of NCCN Recommendations for Early Detection

recommendations.statement: Do not use a prostate cancer risk calculator alone to decide whether biopsy is indicated.
recommendations.context: Clinical judgment and patient preferences must also inform the decision.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The calculators have not been assessed in randomized trials, and risk thresholds linked to reduced mortality are unknown.

recommendations.statement: Follow individuals with low suspicion for clinically significant cancer with PSA and DRE in 6–12 mo.
recommendations.context: This follows further evaluation of a possible biopsy indication.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.source_heading: Further Evaluation and Indications for Biopsy

recommendations.statement: Encourage biopsy when suspicion of clinically significant prostate cancer is high.
recommendations.context: This includes patients with a persistent, substantial PSA increase or higher PSA density, even when MRI is normal.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: A normal MRI cannot reliably exclude clinically significant cancer.
recommendations.source_heading: Further Evaluation and Indications for Biopsy

recommendations.statement: Strongly recommend biopsy for an individual with elevated PSA and an abnormal DRE.
recommendations.context: An examination that is very suspicious for cancer also warrants further evaluation regardless of PSA.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: An abnormal DRE accompanying elevated PSA has high predictive value.

recommendations.statement: Use image-guided biopsy for individuals with high suspicion of clinically significant cancer; MRI targeting is preferred when available.
recommendations.context: Either a transrectal or a transperineal approach is an option, and image-guided biopsy techniques should be used routinely.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: MRI-targeted techniques improve detection of clinically significant disease while reducing detection of lower-risk disease.

recommendations.statement: When systematic prostate biopsy is performed, obtain an extended-pattern biopsy with at least 12 cores.
recommendations.context: The described pattern samples medial and lateral peripheral zones and directs cores toward lesions.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The extended pattern detects more cancer than sextant sampling.

recommendations.statement: Prefer combined targeted and systematic biopsy when MRI targeting is available, at least for an initial biopsy.
recommendations.context: Some clinicians favor omitting systematic cores because of overdiagnosis concerns, but the panel continues to recommend the combined approach.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Systematic sampling uniquely detects some high-grade cancers and contributes to risk stratification.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely include anteriorly directed cores in an initial biopsy; they may be added to an extended repeat-biopsy protocol when PSA remains elevated.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Routine anterior sampling is not supported by the guideline.

recommendations.statement: Consider biomarker tests for an individual thought to remain at higher risk despite a negative prostate biopsy.
recommendations.context: The listed post-biopsy options include percent-free PSA, 4Kscore, PHI, PCA3, ConfirmMDx, ExoDx Prostate Test, MPS, and IsoPSA.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: A negative biopsy does not exclude cancer, and additional tests may help inform a repeat-biopsy decision.

recommendations.statement: After at least 1 negative prostate biopsy, consider mpMRI if it was not previously performed and suspicion of cancer remains high.
recommendations.context: Suspicion may be based on PSA and/or biomarker results.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: mpMRI may reveal regions of cancer missed by earlier sampling.

recommendations.statement: Strongly consider MRI-targeted biopsy techniques after a negative biopsy when concern for cancer persists.
recommendations.context: Persistently elevated or rising PSA and/or biomarker results may support repeat evaluation.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Targeting may identify clinically significant cancer missed on earlier biopsies.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely use a saturation-biopsy strategy for every individual with a prior negative biopsy.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: The guideline favors the demonstrated utility of mpMRI and MRI-targeted biopsy in this population.

recommendations.statement: Consider minor anesthetic techniques for all patients undergoing prostate biopsy.
recommendations.context: The guideline discusses topical lidocaine and injectable nerve blocks; deep sedation or general anesthesia may be advantageous in selected circumstances.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: These measures improve procedural tolerability, particularly with extended or saturation sampling.

recommendations.statement: Refer patients with prostate cancer established on biopsy for comprehensive care under the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer.
recommendations.context: Treatment decisions are outside the scope of this early detection guideline.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Early detection and subsequent selective management are intended to be linked.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely repeat a biopsy after prostate cancer has been diagnosed, except in particular circumstances.
recommendations.context: The specified circumstances include both suspicion of more aggressive disease than the initial biopsy showed and the patient being a candidate for active surveillance.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus

recommendations.statement: When IDC is found on biopsy without invasive carcinoma, recommend proceeding directly to definitive therapy; if that is not pursued, undertake careful evaluation with strong consideration of repeat MRI-targeted biopsy to seek invasive cancer.
recommendations.context: The treatment recommendation refers to the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: IDC in biopsy material strongly suggests associated high-grade cancer.

recommendations.statement: When AIP is identified on biopsy without invasive carcinoma, repeat biopsy using both MRI targeting and systematic sampling to look for invasive carcinoma.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: AIP may indicate unsampled cancer and is associated with increased detection of invasive carcinoma and/or IDC on repeat biopsy.
recommendations.source_heading: Atypical Intraductal Proliferation Without Invasive Cancer

recommendations.statement: After a benign biopsy, atypia suspicious for cancer, or HGPIN, obtain PSA and DRE at 12- to 24-month intervals if a prior high-quality mpMRI was performed; biomarker tests may also be considered.
recommendations.context: A negative prostate biopsy does not exclude cancer.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Follow-up seeks to identify clinically significant cancer while limiting unnecessary testing and overdiagnosis.
recommendations.source_heading: Other Notable Pathologic Features and Benign Results

recommendations.statement: After a benign biopsy, atypia suspicious for cancer, or HGPIN without a prior high-quality mpMRI, consider biomarker testing and/or mpMRI.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Additional assessment may identify risk not resolved by a negative or nonmalignant biopsy result.
recommendations.source_heading: Other Notable Pathologic Features and Benign Results

recommendations.statement: For atypia suspicious for cancer, consider another biopsy in 12–24 months, with relatively greater sampling of the previously atypical site.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: Cancer subsequently found after atypia is most likely to be in the area that initially showed atypia.
recommendations.source_heading: Other Notable Pathologic Features and Benign Results

recommendations.statement: After a benign biopsy, atypia suspicious for cancer, or HGPIN, repeat prostate biopsy with refined techniques if suspicion of cancer is high.
recommendations.context: Findings that heighten suspicion include positive mpMRI, persistently high PSA, shorter PSA doubling time, high PSA density, and/or abnormal DRE.
recommendations.grading_system: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
recommendations.rationale: An earlier nonmalignant biopsy does not rule out prostate cancer.
recommendations.source_heading: Other Notable Pathologic Features and Benign Results

special_populations.considerations: The panel recommends offering baseline PSA testing to healthy, informed individuals aged 45–75 years. If PSA is <1 ng/mL and DRE is normal when performed, repeat testing is recommended at 2- to 4-year intervals. If PSA is 1–3 ng/mL and DRE is normal when performed, the recommended interval is 1 to 2 years.

For healthy, informed individuals aged 40–75 years who are Black/African American, carry germline mutations associated with prostate cancer risk, or have a concerning family or personal history, the panel recommends offering baseline PSA testing. With PSA ≤3 ng/mL and a normal DRE when performed, repeat testing is recommended at 1 to 2-year intervals. Further evaluation can be considered in younger individuals, including those whose PSA exceeds the median for their age group without exceeding >3 ng/mL.

This population has higher prostate cancer incidence and mortality and an earlier age at diagnosis than white individuals. The guideline relates survival disparities to social determinants of health and unequal access to care, rather than race itself. The panel recommends considering shared decision-making about PSA screening at age 40 years and considering annual rather than every-other-year screening. Current evidence does not show that starting before age 45 reduces morbidity or mortality, and earlier screening may increase overdiagnosis.
BRCA2 is associated with increased prostate cancer risk and potentially earlier-onset or lethal disease. The panel recommends prostate cancer early detection beginning at age 40 years.

special_populations.population: Individuals with other germline mutations associated with prostate cancer risk
special_populations.considerations: The panel considers it reasonable to discuss PSA screening starting at age 40 years and to consider annual rather than every-other-year screening. Known or suspected cancer susceptibility genes warrant referral to a cancer genetics professional. The guideline discusses BRCA1, ATM, CHEK2, PALB2, HOXB13, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM, and TP53 among relevant genes, while noting that risks differ by mutation.

The guideline describes a 2- to 5.8-fold increase in prostate cancer risk associated with Lynch syndrome. Age at onset and aggressiveness generally do not appear to differ from sporadic prostate cancer. Germline mutation status should inform discussions about early detection.

The guideline associates this syndrome with an approximately 9-fold increased prostate cancer risk and notes evidence suggesting more aggressive prostate cancer in individuals with germline TP53 mutations. Germline mutation status should inform discussions about early detection.

special_populations.population: Individuals with a suspicious family or personal cancer history
special_populations.considerations: The panel recommends beginning shared decision-making about PSA screening at age 40 years. A suspicious family history warrants genetic testing; when testing does not identify a germline mutation in a prostate cancer risk gene, shared decision-making about the timing and frequency of PSA testing remains recommended. A known or suspected cancer susceptibility gene warrants referral to a cancer genetics professional.

Continuing PSA screening is a category 2B option restricted to selected, very healthy individuals with little or no comorbidity, particularly those never tested or with rising PSA. Widespread testing at this age is not recommended because it would substantially increase overdetection. For those continuing screening who have PSA <4 ng/mL, a normal DRE when performed, and no other biopsy indication, repeat testing at 1- to 3-year intervals or discontinuation when clinically appropriate can be considered. PSA ≥4 ng/mL or a DRE very suspicious for cancer prompts further evaluation. Individuals >75 years with PSA <3.0 ng/mL have a very low lifetime risk of prostate cancer metastases.

special_populations.population: Individuals with a life expectancy of less than 10 years
special_populations.considerations: Panel members unanimously agree that PSA testing should not be offered. Overall health, comorbidities, life expectancy, and individual preferences are central to decisions about early detection.

finasteride and dutasteride typically lower serum PSA by approximately 50% within 6 to 12 months, but the response varies substantially. Medication use and duration should be assessed when interpreting PSA. The guideline cautions that simply doubling a measured PSA can make cancer detection unreliable; a confirmed rise from the post-treatment PSA nadir may better indicate a need for biopsy. A failure to achieve a substantial PSA decrease may warrant regular testing.
Patients with this exposure should be informed that it may be associated with an increased risk of high-grade prostate cancer.

special_populations.population: Individuals with a prior negative prostate biopsy
special_populations.considerations: A negative biopsy does not rule out prostate cancer. Persistent concern based on PSA or biomarker results warrants consideration of mpMRI, biomarker testing, and refined targeted biopsy techniques. For benign results, atypia suspicious for cancer, or HGPIN, follow-up depends on whether a prior high-quality mpMRI was performed: with one, PSA and DRE are recommended at 12- to 24-month intervals; without one, biomarkers and/or mpMRI should be considered. Repeat biopsy is recommended when suspicion of cancer is high.

conditions.name: Prostate cancer
conditions.description: Prostate cancer ranges from slow-growing disease that may not require immediate treatment to aggressive disease that can threaten life. This guideline addresses early detection and decisions about prostate biopsy, not prostate cancer treatment.
conditions.epidemiology: In the United States, prostate cancer accounts for 29% of new cancer diagnoses in males and is the second leading cause of cancer death in American men. For 2024, the cited estimates are 299,010 diagnoses and 35,250 deaths. The lifetime estimates for men in the United States are about 1 chance in 8 (12.9%) of diagnosis and about 1 chance in 41 (2.4%) of death from prostate cancer. U.S. prostate cancer death rates fell by 53% from 1993 to 2018, although they stabilized toward the end of that period. Risk is higher in Black/African American individuals, people with certain germline mutations, and people with a concerning family or personal cancer history.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Early prostate cancer has no identifiable symptoms. Advanced disease may cause urinary obstruction, prostatic bleeding, hematospermia, or bone pain. Lower urinary tract symptoms in people considering screening may instead arise from benign prostatic enlargement.

subtypes.name: Grade Group 1
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Described as lower-risk disease in the biopsy comparisons; a diagnosis may not require immediate treatment.

subtypes.name: Grade Group ≥2
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Used as a threshold for clinically significant or higher-grade disease in several diagnostic studies.

subtypes.name: Grade Group ≥3
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Used to identify higher-risk disease in comparisons of biopsy methods.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess health, life expectancy, preferences, cancer history, inherited risk, prostate disease, prior testing, medications, environmental exposure, and symptoms.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before decisions about participation in early detection.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A concerning family history, relevant germline mutation, or Black/African American identity informs the assessment of elevated risk.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide the principal serum test for early detection and guide the need for further evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As baseline testing in informed, healthy individuals choosing early detection, with timing determined by risk and age; repeat an abnormally high result, particularly near an evaluation threshold.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Risk rises with PSA, but no PSA concentration eliminates cancer risk. PSA >3 ng/mL prompts further evaluation in the principal algorithm; PSA ≥4 ng/mL is the further-evaluation threshold for selected individuals >75 years. Infection, instrumentation, ejaculation, trauma, and medications can affect results. Values from differently calibrated commercial assays are not directly interchangeable.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Complement PSA and help determine whether further assessment or biopsy is warranted.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered at baseline; perform when PSA is elevated if it was not part of the initial assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: DRE should not be used alone for early detection. A finding very suspicious for cancer warrants further evaluation regardless of PSA; an abnormal finding with elevated PSA has greater predictive value.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess noncancer explanations for an elevated PSA.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation before a biopsy decision, particularly with PSA >3 ng/mL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform whether to biopsy and identify areas for targeted sampling.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Strongly recommended before image-guided biopsy if available; also considered after a negative biopsy when suspicion persists and high-quality mpMRI was not previously performed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A negative result does not rule out clinically significant cancer. PSA density and other biomarkers can inform a biopsy decision despite a negative scan. High-quality imaging and radiologic expertise are important.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish PSA elevation associated with prostate enlargement from cancer risk.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider with elevated PSA in a biopsy-naïve individual or when deciding about biopsy after a negative mpMRI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It is calculated as PSA in ng/mL divided by prostate volume in cc; higher values are associated with greater risk of high-grade cancer. Earlier studies used 0.15 ng/mL/g, but later studies questioned that cutoff's sensitivity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Improve the specificity of PSA-based assessment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An option before initial biopsy and after a prior negative biopsy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A lower result is associated with greater prostate cancer risk. The document describes FDA approval for individuals aged ≥50 years with a non-suspicious DRE and PSA between 4 and 10 ng/mL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Refine the likelihood of cancer, including higher-grade disease, before a biopsy decision.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An option before initial biopsy or following a negative biopsy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Combines tPSA, fPSA, and proPSA; studies cited in the guideline report an association with cancer grade.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate the probability of Grade Group ≥2 cancer on biopsy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered before biopsy or after a negative biopsy when clinically significant cancer remains a concern.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Uses fPSA, tPSA, human kallikrein 2 (hK2), intact PSA, age, DRE, and prior biopsy status. No optimal cutoff is established.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help identify clinically significant cancer before biopsy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered in individuals without a prior biopsy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Measures urinary DLX1 and HOXC6 expression after DRE, using KLK3 as an internal reference.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Refine the likelihood of Grade Group ≥2 disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered before an initial or repeat biopsy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Also called EPI; evaluates urinary exosomal PCA3 and ERG RNA normalized to SPDEF.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Refine biopsy decisions concerning clinically significant cancer.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered before biopsy or after a negative biopsy when higher-risk disease remains a concern.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Combines total serum PSA with urinary PCA3 and TMPRSS2:ERG expression after DRE.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the risk of higher-grade cancer before a biopsy decision.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered before biopsy or after a negative biopsy in individuals thought to have increased risk of clinically significant disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A blood assay that separates and detects PSA isoforms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help decide whether a repeat biopsy is appropriate.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An option after a prior negative biopsy; the panel considers it inappropriate for the initial-biopsy setting.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Measures PCA3 in urine obtained after DRE.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further stratify cancer risk after a negative biopsy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered when deciding on repeat biopsy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Assesses promoter hypermethylation of GSTP1, APC, and RASSF1 in previously obtained biopsy tissue.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish a tissue diagnosis and assess cancer grade.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Encouraged when suspicion of clinically significant cancer is high; a transrectal or transperineal approach may be used.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: MRI targeting is preferred when available. The panel favors combining targeted and systematic sampling because some high-grade cancers are detected only systematically.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Sample the prostate and contribute to risk stratification if cancer is found.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When systematic sampling is performed, the panel recommends an extended pattern with at least 12 cores.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A negative biopsy does not exclude cancer on a later biopsy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Sample suspicious regions and improve detection of clinically significant disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When MRI targeting is available, including in selected individuals with a prior negative biopsy and persistent suspicion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Targeting may be cognitive, performed with TRUS-MRI fusion, or undertaken directly under MR guidance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate inherited susceptibility when the family history is suspicious.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For patients with a suspicious family history; referral to a cancer genetics professional is recommended when a susceptibility gene is known or suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A negative result does not remove the need to discuss PSA-testing timing and frequency when family history remains concerning.

diagnostic_workup.test: Sunnybrook-, ERSPC-, and PCPT-based risk calculators
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate the likelihood of biopsy-detectable cancer and high-grade cancer using clinical factors.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May inform discussion about biopsy, but should not alone determine whether biopsy is indicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Their risk cutoffs have not been linked to reduced prostate cancer mortality in randomized trials.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Distinguishes lower-grade findings from clinically significant or higher-risk cancer in biopsy studies; Grade Group ≥2 and Grade Group ≥3 are thresholds used for different study outcomes.
The guideline identifies Gleason score ≥3+4 alongside Grade Group 2 or higher when describing high-grade cancer risk assessment.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Carriers have increased prostate cancer risk, with concern for earlier-onset or potentially lethal disease; early detection is recommended at age 40.

follow_up.schedule: For average-risk individuals aged 45–75 years with PSA <1 ng/mL and a normal DRE if performed, repeat testing at 2- to 4-year intervals; with PSA 1–3 ng/mL, repeat at 1 to 2-year intervals. For higher-risk individuals aged 40–75 years with PSA ≤3 ng/mL and a normal DRE if performed, repeat at 1 to 2-year intervals. In carefully selected individuals >75 years with PSA <4 ng/mL, a normal DRE if performed, and no other biopsy indication, repeat at 1 to 3-year intervals or consider stopping screening when clinically appropriate. When suspicion for clinically significant cancer is low after further evaluation, follow up in 6–12 mo.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: These intervals concern early detection before a cancer diagnosis. The guideline directs care after a cancer diagnosis to the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer.

conditions.name: Intraductal carcinoma (IDC)
conditions.description: An adverse intraductal pathologic finding that may be identified without invasive carcinoma on prostate needle biopsy. Its presence strongly suggests high-grade cancer.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify IDC and establish whether invasive carcinoma is present.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As part of prostate cancer diagnostic evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: IDC without identified invasive carcinoma raises substantial concern for associated high-grade cancer.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Strongly considered if IDC without invasive carcinoma is not followed directly by definitive therapy.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: An independent adverse pathologic factor; on biopsy it strongly suggests associated high-grade cancer.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline recommends proceeding directly to definitive therapy for IDC found without invasive carcinoma; otherwise, careful evaluation with strong consideration of MRI-targeted repeat biopsy is indicated.

conditions.name: Atypical intraductal proliferation (AIP)
conditions.description: An intraductal proliferation with greater architectural complexity and/or cytologic atypia than typical high-grade PIN, without meeting the diagnostic criteria for IDC. On needle biopsy, it may indicate cancer that was not sampled.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify AIP and determine whether invasive carcinoma is present.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation for suspected prostate cancer.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline associates AIP on needle biopsy with increased risk (50%) of invasive carcinoma and/or IDC on repeat biopsy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Search for invasive carcinoma.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Recommended when AIP is identified without invasive carcinoma.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Intraductal architectural complexity and/or cytologic atypia beyond typical high-grade PIN, without fulfilling the diagnostic threshold for IDC.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: May mark unsampled invasive carcinoma and/or IDC.

conditions.name: Atypia, suspicious for cancer

conditions.epidemiology: Approximately 5% of patients have atypia reported on biopsy. The guideline states that cancer is found on repeat biopsy in 50% or more of patients with atypia; the site previously showing atypia is the most likely area of detection.

conditions.description: A prostate biopsy finding whose nuclear features resemble those of malignant tumors, while a basal layer remains present around the acini.
conditions.epidemiology: Approximately 10% of patients undergoing biopsy are found to have HGPIN. Contemporary series using extended biopsy schemes report cancer detection on repeat biopsy of approximately 10% to 20% and occasionally higher; most cancers subsequently detected are low grade.

conditions.description: An inherited cancer syndrome caused by pathogenic germline variants in DNA mismatch repair genes or EPCAM; it is associated predominantly with colorectal and endometrial cancers and also increases prostate cancer risk.

conditions.name: Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer Syndrome
conditions.description: An inherited cancer predisposition associated with germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations; these mutations are also relevant to prostate cancer risk.
conditions.epidemiology: Germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations occur in approximately 0.2% to 0.3% of the general population. BRCA2 mutations are associated with a 2- to 6-fold increase in prostate cancer risk; the association for BRCA1 is less consistent. Prostate cancers in germline BRCA carriers appear to arise earlier, show a more aggressive phenotype, and have significantly shorter survival than those in non-carriers.

subtypes.name: BRCA2 carriers
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline recommends prostate cancer early detection at age 40.

subtypes.name: BRCA1 carriers

document_sections.heading: Updates in Version 2.2024 of the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer Early Detection from Version 1.2024 include:
document_sections.content: The discussion was revised to align with changes to the algorithm.

document_sections.heading: Updates in Version 1.2024 of the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer Early Detection from Version 2.2023 include:
document_sections.content: Revisions addressed concerning family or personal history in risk assessment; consideration of shared decision-making about PSA screening from age 40 years and annual rather than every-other-year screening for Black/African American individuals; further evaluation when PSA exceeds the age-group median despite remaining below >3 ng/mL; testing intervals; mpMRI before biopsy, designated category 1; and image-guided biopsy with MRI targeting preferred. The updates also addressed the interpretation of a suspicious DRE at any PSA level, germline risk genes, disparities affecting Black/African American individuals, and the detection patterns of MRI/ultrasound fusion-guided biopsy.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Prostate cancer ranges from indolent to aggressive disease, and a diagnosis does not always call for immediate treatment. Detecting more early cancers would identify both types. The panel seeks to identify consequential disease while limiting detection and overtreatment of indolent disease, associated morbidity, and harm to quality of life. These guidelines concern early detection, not prostate cancer treatment; treatment recommendations appear in the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer. Early detection should be linked to selective treatment to avoid harm. The intended population comprises individuals with a prostate who choose early detection after counseling about benefits and harms. Most panel members believe that a growing number of diagnosed patients can and should be monitored rather than treated immediately. Most supported the proposed starting and stopping ages, testing intervals, and biopsy indications, but consensus on those particulars was not reached.

document_sections.heading: Baseline Evaluation (PROSD-2)
document_sections.content:
Initial assessment includes history and physical examination: family cancer history; personal or family high-risk germline mutations; prior prostate disease, PSA or PSA isoforms, examinations, and biopsies; Black/African American identity; medications; and environmental exposures. After discussing risks and benefits, obtain baseline PSA and consider baseline DRE. Offer the early-detection discussion at age 40–75 y to those at high risk because of Black/African American identity, risk-associated germline mutations, or concerning family or personal history; for average risk, use age 45–75 y. Screening after age >75 y is confined to selected individuals (category 2B). For average risk with PSA <1 ng/mL and normal DRE, if performed, repeat testing at a 2- to 4-year interval. For high risk with PSA ≤3 ng/mL or average risk with PSA 1–3 ng/mL and normal DRE, if performed, repeat at 1 to 2-year intervals; consider further evaluation in younger patients. PSA >3 ng/mL and/or a very suspicious DRE prompts further evaluation. In selected patients aged >75 y, PSA <4 ng/mL, normal DRE if performed, and no other biopsy indication permit repeat testing at 1 to 3-year intervals or consideration of stopping screening when clinically appropriate; PSA ≥4 ng/mL or a very suspicious DRE prompts further evaluation. Unless specified otherwise, recommendations are category 2A.

If testing identifies no germline mutation in a prostate cancer risk gene but family history remains concerning, shared decision-making about PSA timing and frequency is recommended. Family or personal cancer history and high-risk germline mutations can guide when that discussion begins. Concerning family history includes, without being limited to, a first- or second-degree relative with metastatic prostate cancer; ovarian cancer; breast cancer in a relative assigned male at birth; breast cancer diagnosed at age ≤45 years in a relative assigned female at birth; colorectal or endometrial cancer at ≤50 years; pancreatic cancer; or two or more first- or second-degree relatives with breast, prostate other than clinically localized Grade Group 1, colorectal, or endometrial cancer at any age. Suspicious family history warrants genetic testing. Refer a person with a known or suspected cancer susceptibility gene to a cancer genetics professional. Germline variants may increase lifetime prostate cancer risk and, for certain genes or mutations such as BRCA2, risk of early-onset or potentially lethal disease. Genes listed include BRCA2, BRCA1, ATM, CHEK2, PALB2, HOXB13, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM, and TP53. Early detection is recommended at age 40 years for BRCA2 carriers. For carriers of other germline mutations, considering shared decision-making at age 40 years and annual rather than every-other-year screening is reasonable.

Compared with white individuals, Black/African American individuals have significantly higher prostate cancer incidence and mortality and an earlier age at diagnosis. The guideline attributes this to greater preclinical disease risk and greater likelihood of preclinical spread; it attributes survival disparities to social determinants of health and limited care access, not race itself or differences in tumor-acquired genomic variant frequencies. Data indicate similar outcomes when Black and white patients receive equitable treatment. Appropriate screening and treatment therefore require heightened vigilance. Evidence is limited that beginning earlier reduces morbidity or mortality compared with starting at age 45, and earlier screening may increase overdiagnosis; nevertheless, data indicate greater screening benefit for Black individuals. Many support considering shared decision-making about PSA at age 40 years and annual rather than every-other-year screening. 5g-reductase inhibitors, including finasteride and dutasteride, lower PSA by approximately 50%; their use requires consideration when interpreting PSA. Patients exposed to Agent Orange should be told that exposure may be associated with greater risk of high-grade prostate cancer.

document_sections.heading: PROSD-2B
document_sections.content: Serum PSA has the strongest evidentiary support for early detection. DRE must not be the sole test; it can supplement baseline PSA for all patients and is most useful when PSA is elevated. A DRE suspicious for cancer can justify considering biopsy referral or additional testing at any PSA concentration. After age 75 years, test only exceptionally healthy people with little or no comorbidity, particularly those never tested or whose PSA is rising. Population-wide testing at that age is not recommended because it would markedly increase overdetection. Among people aged 40–49 years, median PSA spans 0.5–0.7 ng/mL and the 75th percentile spans 0.7–0.9 ng/mL. PSA above the age-group median indicates greater risk of prostate cancer and aggressive disease, increasing as PSA rises farther above that median; further evaluation can be considered even below the >3 ng/mL threshold. Lifetime metastatic risk is very low for individuals ≥60 years with PSA <1.0 ng/mL and, especially, those >75 years with PSA <3.0 ng/mL.

document_sections.heading: FURTHER EVALUATION AND INDICATIONS FOR BIOPSY
document_sections.content:
Further assessment includes repeat PSA, DRE if omitted initially, and investigation of benign disease. Obtain mpMRI if available (category 1), and consider biomarkers that increase screening specificity. High suspicion of clinically significant cancer leads to image-guided transrectal or transperineal biopsy, preferably with MRI targeting; biopsy without MRI targeting remains an option. With low suspicion, follow up with PSA and DRE in 6–12 mo. Unless otherwise specified, recommendations are category 2A.

Encourage biopsy for a persistent, substantial PSA rise, including when PSA density is higher, even if MRI is normal. A transperineal TRUS biopsy approach may lower sepsis risk and antibiotic requirements relative to a transrectal approach. In biopsied patients, MRI/ultrasound fusion targeting significantly increases detection of clinically significant, higher-risk Grade Group ≥3 disease while reducing detection of Grade Group 1 or lower-volume Grade Group 2 disease. Routine image-guided biopsy is strongly recommended. High-quality mpMRI equipment and radiologic expertise are essential. Most favor combined targeted and systematic sampling because systematic cores uniquely detect some high-grade cancers and aid risk stratification; others favor omitting systematic cores during MRI targeting because of possible overdiagnosis.

PSA level correlates with cancer risk. PCPT found cancer on end-of-study biopsy in 15% of individuals with PSA ≤4.0 ng/mL and normal DRE; approximately 30% to 35% with PSA between 4 to 10 ng/mL have cancer, while total PSA >10 ng/mL confers a >67% likelihood. Negative MRI does not rule out cancer; biomarkers and/or PSA density can inform a decision against biopsy. Specificity-enhancing biomarkers are not required alongside serum PSA as first-line screening, but can refine risk when biopsy is being considered. Lower percent-free PSA or higher PSA density indicates greater high-grade cancer risk.
