PHI, SelectMDx, 4Kscore, ExoDx Prostate Test, MPS, and IsoPSA may further characterize the probability of Gleason score ≥3+4, Grade Group 2 or higher disease. Validation across diverse populations differs among tests, and their optimal combination with MRI is unknown.

document_sections.heading: MANAGEMENT OF BIOPSY RESULTS
document_sections.content:
Biopsy-confirmed cancer is managed according to the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer. For IDC or AIP without invasive carcinoma, repeat biopsy with MRI targeting and systematic sampling is used to seek invasive carcinoma. After atypia suspicious for cancer, high-grade PIN, or benign findings, subsequent evaluation depends partly on whether a high-quality mpMRI was previously obtained: without one, consider specificity-enhancing biomarkers and/or mpMRI; with one, assess PSA and DRE at 12- to 24-month intervals and consider biomarkers. For atypia, consider another biopsy in 12–24 months with relatively greater sampling of the atypical area. If cancer suspicion is high, repeat biopsy using refined techniques.

IDC independently indicates adverse pathology in radical prostatectomy and needle-biopsy specimens; IDC in a biopsy strongly suggests high-grade cancer. Consider initial treatment or undertake careful evaluation, strongly considering MRI-guided repeat biopsy. AIP can be more architecturally complex or cytologically atypical than high-grade PIN without meeting IDC criteria; on needle biopsy it may indicate unsampled cancer and is associated with an increased risk (50%) of invasive carcinoma and/or IDC at repeat biopsy. A negative biopsy does not exclude cancer on later sampling; follow with PSA and DRE, considering mpMRI and specificity-enhancing biomarkers. PSA screening can be discontinued at certain ages and PSA thresholds. For patients considered at higher risk despite a negative biopsy, consider percent-free PSA, 4Kscore, PHI, PCA3, ConfirmMDx, ExoDx Prostate Test, MPS, or IsoPSA. After at least 1 negative biopsy with persistent high suspicion based on PSA and/or biomarkers, mpMRI and/or refined MRI/ultrasound fusion-guided biopsy are recommended. MRI targeting increases detection of clinically significant higher-risk disease and decreases detection of lower-risk disease. Most favor combining systematic and targeted cores because some high-grade cancers are detected only systematically, although others would omit systematic sampling.

document_sections.heading: NCCN Categories of Evidence and Consensus
document_sections.content: Category 1 denotes high-level evidence and uniform NCCN agreement that an intervention is appropriate. Category 2A denotes lower-level evidence with uniform agreement; Category 2B denotes lower-level evidence with NCCN agreement. Category 3 denotes major NCCN disagreement about appropriateness, regardless of evidence level. Recommendations default to category 2A unless another category is stated.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Prostate cancer ranges from slowly growing disease that may not require treatment to aggressive disease that does. The sequential recommendations seek cancers whose detection could permit effective treatment while minimizing unnecessary procedures and identification of indolent disease. The intended result is less prostate cancer suffering and mortality without avoidable biopsy morbidity, overdiagnosis, or overtreatment. The guidance applies to individuals who elect early detection, not uninformed, unselected population screening. The panel supports early detection only for healthy patients, with decisions informed by individual circumstances and patient preferences.

document_sections.heading: Overview
document_sections.content: Prostate cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in males, accounting for 29% of new diagnoses, and the second leading cause of cancer death in American men. Estimates for 2024 are 299,010 new US diagnoses and 35,250 deaths; nearly 20 million US individuals will face early-detection decisions. Lifetime probabilities for US men are about 1 chance in 8 (12.9%) of diagnosis and about 1 chance in 41 (2.4%) of death. US prostate cancer death rates decreased 53% from 1993 to 2018, largely alongside early detection and better treatment, but stabilized toward the end of that period. The panel supports PSA testing for informed, healthy individuals with a prostate in specified age ranges, citing level I randomized evidence of lower prostate cancer-specific mortality. It also recognizes overdetection and treatment morbidity without benefit for indolent disease. Significant disease should be distinguished from indolent disease, and this guidance should be paired with the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer, which recommend active surveillance or observation for suitable patients.

document_sections.heading: Literature Search Criteria and Guidelines Update Methodology
document_sections.content: Before updating the guideline, a PubMed search combined prostate cancer with screening or early detection. Searches were limited to English-language human studies and selected clinical-trial phases, guidelines, randomized trials, meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and validation studies. The discussion incorporates pertinent PubMed publications and other sources identified by the panel. Where high-level evidence is unavailable, recommendations rely on review of lower-level evidence and expert opinion.

document_sections.heading: Types of Early Detection Testing
document_sections.content: The guideline examines serum PSA and DRE, including test limitations, factors altering PSA, and evidence from screening studies.

document_sections.heading: PSA Testing
document_sections.content: PSA is secreted by prostate epithelial cells; its protease activity liquefies coagulated ejaculate and promotes sperm motility. How it enters the circulation is unknown. Commercial serum assays perform similarly when appropriately used apart from small calibration differences, but results from differently calibrated assays cannot be directly exchanged. Repeat an unusually high result, especially near an evaluation threshold; in one study, approximately 25% initially measuring 4 to 10 ng/mL had a normal repeat result. PSA is not specific to cancer: most people with elevated values do not have prostate cancer, and no low value eliminates risk. Total PSA >10 ng/mL corresponds to greater than 67% likelihood of biopsy-detectable cancer; about 18% with PSA 4 to 10 ng/mL have a subsequent positive biopsy. In PCPT data from 18,882 participants, end-of-study biopsy identified cancer in 15% with PSA of 4.0 ng/mL or less and normal DRE. At 3.1 ng/mL, sensitivity for any prostate cancer was about 32% and specificity about 87%. Appropriate PSA testing alone can advance diagnosis by 5 to 10 years, with variation across studies, populations, and protocols. After PSA testing was introduced, detection shifted toward early organ-confined disease and away from metastasis at diagnosis. Population-screening studies have demonstrated survival benefits using PSA, sometimes alongside DRE or other tests.

document_sections.heading: Factors Affecting PSA Levels
document_sections.content: Infection, recent instrumentation, ejaculation, and trauma can raise PSA; empiric antibiotics appear to add little to test performance in asymptomatic patients with elevated PSA. finasteride and dutasteride, 5-ARIs used for BPH-related lower urinary tract symptoms, typically lower serum PSA by approximately 50% within 6 to 12 months, but responses vary substantially. In one study at 12 months, only 35% had the expected 40% to 60% decline and another 30% had a decrease greater than 60%. Ask about use and duration: simply doubling a measured PSA may make cancer detection unreliable. Failure of PSA to decline substantially while taking 5-ARIs can signal increased risk requiring regular testing; a confirmed rise from the post-treatment nadir may better indicate biopsy than doubling PSA, although reflex ranges have not been established. Several trials suggest enhanced PSA predictive capacity during 5-ARI treatment. In PCPT, involving 18,882 participants, finasteride reduced prostate cancer incidence by 25% versus placebo; the reduction remained 21% through 16 years and involved almost exclusively Grade Group 1 tumors, while the proportion of Grade Group ≥2 tumors increased. At 18 years, neither overall survival nor survival following prostate cancer diagnosis differed significantly from control. After median follow-up of 18.4 years, fewer prostate cancer deaths occurred with finasteride, but that difference was not statistically significant; the investigators' results do not support earlier fears of increased prostate cancer mortality. In REDUCE, dutasteride reduced overall diagnoses by 23% versus control while PSA detected more high-grade tumors in its arm; as in PCPT, the difference in high-grade detection did not produce a mortality difference. A CombAT report found 40% lower incidence with dutasteride plus tamsulosin than tamsulosin alone, with a slightly better yield from PSA-driven biopsy and no increase in diagnoses of Grade Group ≥2 tumors. A population-based study of 333,820 participants associated 5-ARI exposure with lower overall and Grade Group ≤3 cancer risk, with greater reductions after longer treatment; Grade Group 4–5 risk was unchanged. Together these studies suggest greater PSA specificity during finasteride or dutasteride use. Conversely, a cohort analysis of more than 80,000 prostate cancer records associated prediagnostic 5-ARI use with later diagnosis, higher stage, greater prostate cancer-specific mortality, and greater all-cause mortality. Chemoprevention decisions fall outside this guideline. finasteride at 1 mg/day for hair loss also reduces PSA. ketoconazole inhibits androgen synthesis and can lower PSA; recent use belongs in the history. Herbal supplement composition and individual PSA effects are poorly understood. In a survey of 12,457 screening-clinic visitors, greater than 20% used herbal supplements, versus 10% using a prescription lower-urinary-tract-symptom medication; supplements such as saw palmetto may contain PSA-affecting phytoestrogens.

document_sections.heading: Controversies of PSA Testing
document_sections.content: Who should undergo early detection, when to begin, and how often to test remain disputed. PSA screening contributed to a shift toward earlier-stage diagnoses, and metastatic disease at diagnosis has fallen markedly since 1988; its contribution to reduced mortality is likely but not certain. Some assess the benefit as moderate at best because screening can discover disease that would never cause problems, prompting treatment unlikely to provide clinical benefit. Active surveillance for early-stage disease has increased significantly, easing earlier overtreatment concerns. False-positive PSA findings can cause anxiety, costs, and biopsy complications. In 2012, USPSTF advised against routine PSA testing; subsequently, screening, biopsies, localized diagnoses, and radical prostatectomies declined. Whether that recommendation altered metastatic diagnoses remains unclear because studies disagree.

document_sections.heading: DRE with PSA Testing
document_sections.content: USPSTF's 2018 update advised against PSA-based screening at age ≥70 years and advised informed, individualized decisions at age 55 to 69 years, including discussion of benefits and harms; it gave no direction for people <55 years. Data suggest PSA testing increased after that revision. Whether to include baseline DRE is disputed. In a trial of approximately 36,000 participants, 3568 received a prostate cancer diagnosis and 2233 underwent radical prostatectomy. Among those 2233, DRE alone identified 303 (14%), including 60 (3%) with non-organ–confined disease and 56 (3%) with clinical Grade Group >2. Clinically significant disease identified by DRE among people with PSA <3 ng/mL might therefore represent around 0.2% of everyone screened. SEER data on 166,104 diagnosed individuals from 2004 to 2007 identified 685 (0.4%) with palpable, PSA-occult disease at PSA <2.5 ng/mL and Grade Group ≥4. DRE alone is not appropriate for early detection: it misses many significant cancers, has poor PPV, and the cancers it alone detects are less often organ-confined than PSA-detected cancers. In PLCO, which combined DRE and PSA in 35,350 participants, 15.4% of those with abnormal DRE also had elevated PSA. Suspicious DRE was associated with clinically significant cancer (HR, 2.21; 95% CI, 1.99–2.44; P < .001) and prostate cancer-specific death (HR, 2.54; 95% CI, 1.41–4.58; P = .002); corresponding associations for PSA were HR, 5.48; 95% CI, 5.05–5.96; P < .001 and HR, 5.23; 95% CI, 3.08–8.88; P < .001. Combined tests detected more cancer than PSA alone. A prospective study of 6630 individuals reported detection of 3.2% with DRE, 4.6% with PSA, and 5.8% with both. PROBASE randomized 46,642 people aged 45 years between immediate PSA and immediate DRE with PSA deferred until 50 years. In the immediate-PSA group of 23,301, confirmatory testing found PSA ≥3 ng/mL in 186 (0.80%); 120 underwent biopsy, and 48 had cancer (detection rate, 0.2%), including four Grade Group ≥3 cancers. In the delayed-PSA group of 23,194, 6537 accepted initial DRE, yielding 57 suspicious findings, 37 biopsies, and two Grade Group 1 diagnoses. This supports the ineffectiveness of DRE alone. Among 5519 PCPT control participants, abnormal DRE increased cancer detection probability almost 2.5-fold and high-grade disease risk 2.7fold in multivariable analysis. PLCO analysis associated suspicious DRE with Grade Group ≥2 cancer at PSA ≥3 ng/mL: 23.0% risk at 10 years versus 13.7% with nonsuspicious DRE. At PSA <2 ng/mL the corresponding risks were 1.5% versus 0.7%; at PSA 2 to 3 ng/mL they were 6.5% versus 3.5%. Another study also found greater cancer likelihood with positive DRE when PSA was >3 ng/mL. At normal PSA, DRE PPV is about 4%–21%. The panel permits DRE alongside PSA after an asymptomatic individual chooses screening following a benefit-risk discussion; abnormal DRE alone at low PSA could otherwise trigger many unnecessary biopsies and insignificant diagnoses. A very suspicious DRE warrants further evaluation irrespective of PSA, and DRE should be performed when PSA is elevated to help decide about biopsy.

document_sections.heading: Population-Based Screening Studies
document_sections.content: The guideline evaluates randomized PSA-screening evidence and its limitations, including differences between organized screening and usual-care testing.

document_sections.heading: ERSPC Trial
document_sections.content: ERSPC randomized about 182,000 participants aged 50 to 74 years in seven European countries to offered PSA screening, on average once every 4 years, or no such offer; the screened group could also receive DRE or ancillary tests. Its predefined core comprised 162,388 aged 55 to 69 years, and prostate cancer death was the primary outcome. At median follow-up of 11 years, cumulative incidence was 7.4% with screening versus 5.1% in control; prostate cancer deaths numbered 299 versus 462. The screening-to-control prostate cancer death rate ratio was 0.79 (95% CI, 0.68–0.91; P = .001). Investigators concluded that PSA screening lowered disease-specific mortality by 21% and estimated that 1055 needed screening and 37 additional people needed treatment over 11 years to avert one death. Modeling by Heijnsdijk and colleagues instead estimated 98 needed screening and 5 needed treatment. At 13-year follow-up, 7408 screening-arm participants and 6107 controls had prostate cancer; the unadjusted mortality rate ratio was 0.79 (95% CI, 0.69–0.91), and the ratio adjusted for nonparticipation was 0.73 (95% CI, 0.61–0.88). Investigators estimated that inviting 781 people or diagnosing 27 additional cancers would avert one prostate cancer death. Another analysis of those 13-year data reported fewer metastatic diagnoses with screening (incidence rate ratio, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.52–0.70). By 16 years, the corresponding numbers invited and additionally diagnosed per death averted were 570 and 18. Rotterdam ERSPC analysis reported a 32% reduction in prostate cancer-specific mortality; after accounting for contamination and nonattendance, its investigators estimated a possible reduction of up to 51%. The Finnish component reported a small, non-statistically significant disease-specific mortality reduction after 12 years.

document_sections.heading: Population-Based Screening Studies
document_sections.content: The Göteborg randomized population study began independently of ERSPC, although some participants also contributed to ERSPC. It allocated 20,000 people aged 50 to 64 years to PSA invitations every 2 years until age 69 years or control; 76% of the invited group attended at least once. Population PSA use started at 3% and increased. At median follow-up of 14 years, diagnoses numbered 1138 with screening versus 718 with control; cumulative incidences were 12.7% versus 8.2% (HR, 1.64; 95% CI, 1.50–1.80; P < .0001). The disease-specific death rate ratio was 0.56 (95% CI, 0.39–0.82; P = .002). The study estimated 293 people screened and 12 diagnosed per prostate cancer death prevented over 14 years. At 18 years, diagnoses numbered 1396 versus 962; the reported absolute prostate cancer-specific mortality reduction was 0.72 (95% CI, 0.50–0.94), with 139 invitations and 13 diagnoses needed to prevent one death. Possible explanations for its more favorable findings include younger age, less control-group screening contamination, a lower biopsy threshold, and more frequent or prolonged screening. Because more than half its participants were included in ERSPC's principal analysis, Göteborg is not an independent confirmatory study. An analysis found screening and control risks of aggressive cancer and disease-specific mortality converged 9 years after screening stopped. Screening benefit was observed without immediate treatment of every detected cancer, consistent with selective risk-based treatment.

document_sections.heading: PLCO Trial
document_sections.content: PLCO randomized 76,685 individuals aged 55 to 74 years at 10 US centers to annual screening—PSA for 6 years and DRE for 4 years—or usual care. At 13 years, the screened-to-control incidence rate ratio was 1.12 (95% CI, 1.07–1.17), without a statistically significant disease-specific mortality difference (RR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.87–1.36); findings were similar at 15 years. Interpretation is limited by screening before enrollment and 40% to 52% yearly control-group contamination: 74% of usual-care participants were screened at least once. Estimated mean PSA tests and DREs were 2.7 and 1.1 in controls versus 5.0 and 3.5 with organized screening. Biopsy uptake following elevated PSA was also relatively low. Accordingly, PLCO largely contrasted scheduled with opportunistic screening rather than screening with no screening, although it suggests that annual testing may offer limited value compared with less frequent testing. An analysis adjusting for screening and workup in PLCO and ERSPC control arms estimated prostate cancer death-risk reductions of 25% to 31% and 27% to 32%, respectively. A PLCO subgroup analysis reported 44% lower disease-specific death risk with screening among people with no or minimal comorbidity, with 723 needing screening and 5 needing treatment to avert one death; it found no such benefit with one or more significant comorbidities. Other investigators caution that this subgroup approach may have major methodological errors.

document_sections.heading: CAP Trial
document_sections.content: CAP randomized participants aged 50 to 69 years (n = 419,582) to one PSA test or no screening. At median follow-up of 10 years, prostate cancer deaths were 549 versus 647 (P = .50), without an all-cause mortality difference; the tested arm had more low-risk diagnoses. Limitations include use of a single PSA test, standard 10-core biopsy, 10 years of median follow-up, and intervention completion by only 40% of participants. Repeated tests, greater biopsy completion, longer observation, or additional prebiopsy technology might have yielded more benefit.

document_sections.heading: Trial Limitations
document_sections.content: The randomized studies did not establish screening benefit in high-risk groups: less than 5% of PLCO participants had African descent and only 7% reported a prostate cancer family history. Many participants received sextant rather than current extended-core biopsy. ERSPC benefit may have been underestimated because the first PSA test occurred at median age >60 years, screening was generally every 4 years, and treatment available in Europe in the 1990s may have been less effective than current treatment. Mortality benefit must be weighed against treatment harms, favoring selective over universal treatment after screen detection.

document_sections.heading: Practical Considerations of Testing
document_sections.content: The guideline considers when to start, repeat, and end PSA testing in light of individual risk, competing mortality, and overdiagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Age at Which to Initiate Testing
document_sections.content: The ideal starting age remains disputed. Mortality trials focused chiefly on ages 55 to 69 years; ERSPC and Göteborg found disease-specific mortality reductions at ages 55 to 69 and 50 to 64 years, respectively. They support baseline testing at age 50 to 55 years, with the strongest evidence at age 55 years. People <50 years were excluded from these screening trials, so earlier baseline testing lacks randomized evaluation; observational work in the 40s and early 50s suggests risk-stratification value that some regard as marginal, with potential unnecessary biopsies and overdiagnosis. Lilja and colleagues evaluated blood from 21,277 Swedish participants aged 33 to 50 years followed until 2006; among 1312 cases and 3728 controls, one PSA assessment before age 50 years predicted cancer up to 30 years later, with AUC 0.72, or 0.75 for advanced disease. Another study linked baseline PSA at ages 45 to 49 years and 51 to 55 years strongly with future death; 44% of cohort deaths arose in the highest PSA tenth, supporting consideration of baseline testing below age 55. In the Physicians' Health Study nested case-control sample aged 40 to 59 years, baseline PSA predicted later lethal disease; at ages 55 to 59 years, PSA above the 90th percentile versus at or below the median yielded OR 6.9 (95% CI, 2.5–19.1). A PLCO secondary analysis in people aged 55 to 60 years found actuarial clinically significant cancer incidence at 13 years of 0.4% (95% CI, 0%–0.8%) for baseline PSA ≤0.49 ng/mL, 1.5% (95% CI, 1.1%–1.9%) for 0.50–0.99 ng/mL, 5.4% (95% CI, 4.4%–6.4%) for 1.00–1.99 ng/mL, 10.6% (95% CI, 8.3%–12.9%) for 2.00–2.99 ng/mL, 15.3% (95% CI, 11.4%–19.2%) for 3.00–3.99 ng/mL, and 29.5% (95% CI, 24.2%–34.8%) for ≥4.00 ng/mL (all pairwise log-rank P ≤ .004). Baseline PSA can therefore help determine subsequent testing frequency and predicts future disease more strongly than family history or African ancestry. Most panelists favor informed testing from age 45 years at average risk and consideration of shared decision-making from age 40 for Black/African American individuals, carriers of risk-associated germline mutations, and those with concerning family or personal history.

document_sections.heading: Frequency of Testing
document_sections.content: The interval best balancing mortality benefit against overdiagnosis is uncertain. In a comparison of Göteborg's 4202 participants screened every 2 years and Rotterdam's 13,301 screened every 4 years at ages 55 to 64 years, with 11 to 12 years of similar follow-up, biennial screening produced a significant 43% reduction in advanced diagnoses—clinical stage >T3a, N1, or M1; PSA >20 ng/mL; or Grade Group 5 at biopsy—but a 46% increase in low-risk diagnoses—stage T1c, Gleason <6, and PSA <10 ng/mL at biopsy. Very low PSA can support longer intervals: in Rotterdam, PSA below 1 ng/mL was associated with cancer risk of 0.23% at 4 years and 0.49% at 8 years. At age 60 years in a Swedish case-control study of 1167 individuals, PSA ≤1 ng/mL corresponded to 0.5% metastatic risk by age 85 and 0.2% prostate cancer death risk; other cohorts similarly link low age-relative PSA with low risks. Risk increases as PSA exceeds the age-group median. An unscreened-versus-regularly-screened Malmö cohort comparison concluded that testing harms outweigh benefits for PSA <1 ng/mL at age 60 years, approximately 50% of the population. Its authors projected 171 additional diagnoses per 10,000 individuals over 15 years from testing every 2 years in that group, without a concurrent mortality reduction. Microsimulation suggests risk-adjusted intervals can reduce testing burden while retaining survival gains. One model projected prostate cancer death risk of 2.27% with biennial testing at average PSA and testing every 5 years below the decade-specific age median, versus 2.86% without screening. Relative to annual screening at a 4.0 ng/mL biopsy threshold, this strategy projected overdiagnosis of 2.4% versus 3.3%, 59% fewer total tests, and 50% fewer false positives; findings remained robust in sensitivity analyses varying cancer incidence and screening-attributed survival. A model in Black individuals suggested shorter intervals might reduce mortality without increasing overdiagnosis. The panel recommends repeat testing every 2- to 4-years for average risk with PSA <1 ng/mL, and every 1- to 2-years for high risk with PSA ≤3 ng/mL or average risk with PSA 1–3 ng/mL. Consider further evaluation for younger people or PSA above the age median even below >3 ng/mL. For selected exceptionally healthy people >75 years with PSA <4 ng/mL, recommend repeat testing at 1 to 3-year intervals or consider clinically appropriate discontinuation. Select an interval within these ranges using clinical judgment and shared decisions.

document_sections.heading: Age at Which to Discontinue Testing
document_sections.content: Because ERSPC, PLCO, and Göteborg observed testing benefit only through age 70 years, several panelists favored stopping then. Other observational data suggest potential benefit after 70 years but have interpretive limitations. Among 4561 radical-prostatectomy patients, those >70 years had higher grade and stage and worse survival than those ≤70 years. SEER analyses found disease-specific death of 21% after diagnosis at >70 years versus 17% after diagnosis at <70 years, and more advanced disease and prostate cancer death after diagnosis at ≥75 years than before age 75 years despite more competing deaths. A Swedish cohort found similar patterns but indicated that older patients might receive insufficient evaluation or curative care; less prior PSA screening among those >70 years could also contribute to more advanced diagnoses. The panel unanimously advises against PSA testing when life expectancy is less than 10 years. The optimal stopping age for asymptomatic people with normal PSA remains unknown. A microsimulation model predicted that lowering stopping age from 74 to 69 years would reduce the probability of a life saved by 27% relatively while reducing overdiagnosis probability by almost 50%. Screening through age 74 years with an age-increasing biopsy PSA threshold reduced overdiagnosis by one third versus a uniform 4.0 ng/mL cutoff, with little change in lives saved. At age 60 years, baseline PSA <1 ng/mL was associated in a study with 0.5% metastatic risk and 0.2% prostate cancer death risk. In a BLSA study of 849 individuals, no participant aged 75 to 80 years with PSA <3.0 ng/mL died of prostate cancer; time to death or aggressive diagnosis was longer below than above PSA 3.0 ng/mL. People ≥60 years with PSA <1.0 ng/mL and those >75 years with PSA <3.0 ng/mL have very low metastatic risk. Continue screening beyond 75 years only cautiously in exceptionally healthy people with little or no comorbidity, especially those never tested or with rising PSA (category 2B); broad testing is not recommended because overdetection would rise substantially. For those >75 years choosing continued early detection (category 2B), PSA <4 ng/mL, normal DRE if performed, and no other biopsy indication permit testing every 1- to 3-years or consideration of stopping when appropriate. PSA ≥4 ng/mL or a very suspicious DRE calls for further evaluation.

document_sections.heading: Screening in Populations with Elevated Risk
document_sections.content: Concerning family or personal history, Black/African American identity, and certain germline variants increase prostate cancer risk. Exposure to the Agent Orange constituent TCDD may also be linked to prostate cancer; inform exposed patients that their risk of high-grade disease may be increased.

document_sections.heading: Family History
document_sections.content: A first-degree relative diagnosed before age 60 raises the likelihood of a prostate cancer diagnosis 2.1- to 2.5-fold. A sibling with aggressive disease was associated with aggressive disease OR 1.21 (95% CI, 1.04–1.39). A Swedish population study found risk increasing with the number of affected relatives. Available data nevertheless suggest familial prostate cancer is not necessarily more aggressive and that cancer-specific outcomes resemble those without a family history. Breast cancer family history also raises prostate cancer risk. Assess relevant personal and family cancers and undertake genetic testing for suspicious family history. Familial risk estimates may be inflated because relatives of affected patients undergo more screening and biopsy.

document_sections.heading: Genetic Syndromes
document_sections.content: Ask about known personal or familial germline mutations associated with increased cancer risk; refer known or suspected susceptibility-gene carriers to a cancer genetics professional. Refer patients meeting criteria in the NCCN hereditary-risk assessment guidelines for genetic counseling or testing when appropriate. Available commercial panels assess genes including BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, HOXB13, CHEK2, NBN, PALB2, RAD51D, and TP53. Reported germline DNA-repair alterations among patients with prostate cancer include BRCA2 (5%), ATM (2%), CHEK2 (2%), BRCA1 (1%), RAD51D (0.4%), PALB2 (0.4%), ATR (0.3%), and NBN, PMS2, GEN1, MSH2, MSH6, RAD51C, MRE11A, BRIP1, or FAM175A. Such inherited alterations may confer higher risk. Rare HOXB13 G84E confers significantly greater prostate cancer risk and more early-onset familial disease; HOXB13 variants occur more often in Scandinavian-heritage families, while rare HOXB13 X285K has been found in people of West African ancestry and may also increase risk. Include high-risk mutation status in early-detection discussions because carriers may not recognize its implications.

document_sections.heading: Lynch Syndrome
document_sections.content: Lynch syndrome arises from pathogenic germline variants in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM. Although chiefly associated with colorectal and endometrial cancer, it is also associated with 2- to 5.8-fold greater prostate cancer risk. Age at onset and aggressiveness generally appear similar to sporadic prostate cancer. A study of 524 families with pathogenic germline PALB2 alterations found no evidence of higher prostate cancer risk. IMPACT enrolled carriers aged 40 to 69 years of MLH1, MSH2, or MSH6 mutations (n = 644), related age-matched noncarriers (n= 184), and an additional 134 randomly selected noncarriers from its BRCA1/2 cohort. Participants were assigned annual PSA testing for at least 5 years. After the first round, prostate cancer incidence was 4.3% among MSH2 carriers (13 of 305; 95% CI, 2.3–7.2), 3.0% among MSH6 carriers (4 of 135; 95% CI, 0.8–7.4), and 0.5% among MSH2 noncarrier controls (1 of 210; 95% CI, 0–2.6); no MLH1 carrier or other noncarrier control received a diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Li-Fraumeni Syndrome
document_sections.content: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) results from a pathogenic TP53 germline variant and raises risk for multiple primary cancers, most commonly breast cancer, osteosarcoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, CNS tumors, and soft-tissue sarcoma. It is also associated with approximately 9-fold higher prostate cancer risk; data additionally suggest more aggressive prostate cancer among TP53 germline carriers.

document_sections.heading: Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer Syndrome
document_sections.content:
Germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants occur in approximately 0.2% to 0.3% of the general population, at differing rates across racial or ethnic groups, and numerous reports associate them with higher prostate cancer risk. BRCA2 variants are linked to a 2- to 6-fold increase, whereas findings for BRCA1 are less consistent. Prostate cancers in germline BRCA carriers appear earlier and more aggressive and are associated with significantly shorter survival than cancers in noncarriers. In interim IMPACT findings, participants aged 40 to 69 years included 919 BRCA1 carriers, 902 BRCA2 carriers, 709 related BRCA1 noncarriers, and 497 related BRCA2 noncarriers; all had annual PSA testing four times. BRCA1 carriers and noncarriers did not differ. Compared with BRCA2 noncarriers, BRCA2 carriers had higher cancer incidence (19.4 per 1000 person years vs. 12.0; P = .03), younger age at diagnosis (61 vs. 64 years; P = .04), and more clinically significant disease (77% vs. 40%; P = .01). Biopsy completion differed between BRCA2 carriers and noncarriers (73% vs. 60%), limiting interpretation. Longer follow-up is needed to determine this early-detection strategy's clinical utility.

In interim results reported in 2019 from the prospective IMPACT study, participants aged 40 to 69 years included 919 BRCA1 carriers, 902 BRCA2 carriers, 709 related BRCA1 non-carriers, and 497 related BRCA2 non-carriers. Participants received annual PSA testing four times. Outcomes did not differ between BRCA1 carriers and non-carriers. Compared with BRCA2 non-carriers, BRCA2 carriers had a higher prostate cancer incidence rate (19.4 per 1000 person years vs. 12.0; P = .03), were younger at diagnosis (61 vs. 64 years; P = .04), and more often had clinically significant disease (77% vs. 40%; P = .01). Biopsy completion was higher among BRCA2 carriers (73% vs. 60%), limiting interpretation. Longer follow-up is needed to establish the clinical usefulness of this early detection approach.

document_sections.heading: African Ancestry
document_sections.content: Compared with white individuals, Black individuals and those with African ancestry have a 60% higher prostate cancer incidence and a 36% to 39% increase in prostate cancer mortality. Black individuals are more likely to present with aggressive or more advanced disease. Modeling suggests more preclinical disease and greater metastatic progression. An analysis of SEER data from 2004 to 2011 found a lower likelihood of treatment among Black individuals even with high-risk disease; treatment became less likely as disease severity increased. Autopsy findings suggest earlier progression to aggressive disease in Black/African American individuals. SEER analyses estimated diagnosis at an adjusted average of 1.2 years younger in non-Hispanic African American than non-Hispanic white American individuals using 2010 data, and an average of 3 years younger in an older analysis. A retrospective population-based United Kingdom cohort estimated an adjusted average difference of 5.1 years. Another study estimated an almost 2-fold greater likelihood of diagnosis before age 45 for African American than white American people. In a Veterans Affairs study of 41,250 individuals, the PSA threshold that best predicted diagnosis within 4 years was lower for African American than white American individuals (1.9 vs. 2.5 ng/mL). In the Southern Community Cohort Study, Black individuals with PSA above the 90th percentile at ages 40 to 64 years had a greatly increased risk of aggressive disease relative to those below the median. Another analysis found a more favorable balance of screening harms and benefits in Black individuals than in all races combined; modeling suggested that shorter testing intervals could lower mortality without raising overdiagnosis in Black individuals. Likely contributors to inequities include lower screening and diagnostic rates, poorer access and insurance coverage, environmental exposures, care-related behaviors, diagnostic delays, and suboptimal treatment. Evidence does not attribute survival inequities to race itself or to the frequency of tumor-acquired genomic variants; outcomes are similar when Black and white patients receive equitable treatment. The panel recommends that Black/African American individuals consider shared decision-making about PSA screening from age 40 years and consider annual rather than every-other-year testing.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations for Early Detection in Populations with Elevated Risk
document_sections.content: Screening evidence comes predominantly from white populations. Non-Hispanic Black participants comprised approximately 4.4% of PLCO, in which 6.9% reported a positive family history but no subgroup analyses were conducted; ERSPC did not report ancestry or family history. The panel considers Black/African American individuals, people with a suspicious personal or family cancer history, and people with a known genetic predisposition to be at high risk. Available evidence is insufficient to determine definitively the best early detection strategy for these groups. Based on evidence and panel consensus, early detection is recommended at age 40 for BRCA2 carriers. People with other germline mutations may reasonably consider shared decision-making about PSA screening at age 40 years and annual rather than every-other-year screening. Those with a suspicious family cancer history should begin shared decision-making at age 40 years. Black/African American individuals may reasonably consider that discussion at age 40 and annual instead of less frequent screening. There is no current evidence that testing people of African descent earlier reduces morbidity or mortality compared with starting at age 45; earlier testing may increase overdiagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Pre-Biopsy Workup
document_sections.content: The panel does not consider DRE alone an absolute biopsy indication when PSA is low, because its positive predictive value in that setting is poor. Nevertheless, a DRE highly suspicious for cancer may indicate high-grade disease even with normal PSA; biopsy can be considered using clinical judgment. For PSA >3 ng/mL, the panel recommends evaluation for benign disease, repeat PSA, and DRE if not already performed before deciding on image-guided biopsy or further biomarker and/or multiparametric MRI assessment. It strongly recommends multiparametric MRI (category 1) before biopsy when available and recommends considering specificity-enhancing biomarkers beforehand. Biomarker predictive performance has not been consistently correlated with multiparametric MRI performance, so their optimal combination is uncertain. With elevated PSA and an abnormal DRE, the panel strongly recommends biopsy because that finding has high predictive value.

document_sections.heading: Further Evaluation and Indications for Biopsy
document_sections.content: Randomized trials used varying PSA thresholds to prompt biopsy. Although 2.5 ng/mL has commonly been used, trial evidence supports 3 ng/mL and its potential to limit overdiagnosis more effectively. For people continuing screening beyond age 75 years, the recommended threshold is 4 ng/mL. Some panel members oppose restricting biopsy consideration to fixed PSA thresholds because age, ancestry, family history, and PSA kinetics also matter. If suspicion of clinically significant cancer is low, follow-up with PSA and DRE is advised in 6 to 12 months. Patients with high suspicion should be encouraged to undergo biopsy.

document_sections.heading: Risk Calculators
document_sections.content: The Sunnybrook-, ERSPC-, and PCPT-based risk calculators combine factors such as age, family history, ancestry, DRE, and PSA to estimate the likelihood of biopsy-detectable prostate cancer and high-grade disease. They may support informed decisions, including decisions to avoid biopsy. They have not been evaluated in RCTs, and risk thresholds associated with reduced prostate cancer mortality are unknown. The panel does not recommend using a calculator alone to decide on biopsy; clinical judgment and patient preferences must also be considered.

document_sections.heading: Magnetic Resonance Imaging
document_sections.content: Pre-biopsy multiparametric MRI may help select patients for biopsy, and MRI during biopsy may guide sampling. Intended benefits are fewer biopsies, less detection of indolent disease and consequent overdiagnosis or overtreatment, and better detection of clinically significant cancer. In PROMIS, 576 previously unbiopsied participants with elevated PSA <15 ng/mL underwent multiparametric MRI, TRUS biopsy, and perineal template mapping biopsy. The template method found clinically significant cancer, defined as Grade Group ≥3 or maximum cancer core length ≥6 mm, in 40%. MRI sensitivity was 93% (95% CI, 88%–96%) versus 48% (95% CI, 42%–55%; P < .0001) for TRUS biopsy, while specificity was 41% (95% CI, 36%–46%) versus 96% (94%–98%; P < .0001). The ≥6 mm definition may be questioned. Using a normal MRI to rule out biopsy would have spared 27%; PROMIS did not test MRI-targeted biopsy directly. In the randomized noninferiority PRECISION trial, 500 participants at 25 centers in 11 countries received an MRI-based pathway or a 10- to 12-core TRUS biopsy. Normal MRI (PI-RADS <3) allowed 28% in the MRI arm to avoid biopsy. Clinically significant cancer detection was 38% with the MRI pathway and 26% with standard biopsy, while 13% fewer MRI-arm participants received a low-risk diagnosis. Results from predominantly European MRI-expert centers may not generalize; other studies also support fewer negative biopsies and indolent diagnoses with pre-biopsy MRI. MRI-FIRST assessed 251 participants at 16 French centers with MRI, systematic biopsy, and targeted biopsy when MRI was abnormal. Among 53 (21%) with normal MRI (Likert 1–2), five (11%) had clinically significant cancer on systematic biopsy. Detection of Grade Group ≥2 cancer was 29.9% (95% CI, 24.3–36.0) with systematic biopsy, 32.3% (95% CI, 26.5–38.4) with targeted biopsy, and 37% with both; targeted and systematic yields did not differ significantly (P = .38). Omitting systematic biopsy would have missed clinically significant cancer in 5.2%, versus 7.6% if targeted biopsy were omitted. Targeting methods varied, MRI was interpreted locally, experienced centers performed the study, two centers enrolled 36%, and agreement between readers was not assessed. In the Dutch 4M study of 626 biopsy-naïve patients at four centers, all received pre-biopsy MRI and systematic biopsy; abnormal scans prompted in-bore targeted biopsy. Two experienced radiologists centrally reviewed scans. MRI was normal (PI-RADS 1–2) in 49% and indeterminate (PI-RADS 3) in 6%. Grade Group ≥2 detection was 30% with combined sampling, 25% with targeting, and 23% with systematic biopsy; the targeted-versus-systematic difference was 2% (95% CI, -1 to 5). Targeting detected less insignificant cancer (difference, 11%; 95% CI, 7–14). Omitting biopsy after PI-RADS 1–2 would have missed 4% of clinically significant cancers found systematically. Among 317 with abnormal MRI, 21 (7%) had cancer found only systematically. The authors describe expert-dependent, potentially non-generalizable conditions. STHLM3-MRI randomized 1532 Swedish individuals with PSA ≥3 ng/mL in a 2:3 ratio to standard biopsy (n = 603) or MRI with targeted and standard biopsy if suggestive of cancer; the MRI approach found fewer clinically insignificant cancers and was noninferior for clinically significant cancer. In the Trio study, 2103 patients with MRI-visible lesions underwent targeted and systematic biopsy. Targeting detected significantly fewer Grade Group 1 and more Grade Group ≥3 cancers than systematic biopsy (P < .01 for all comparisons). Among 404 later undergoing radical prostatectomy, upgrading to Grade Group ≥3 occurred in 16.8% after systematic biopsy, 8.7% after targeted biopsy, and 3.5% after combined biopsy. Combining methods yielded 59 additional Grade Group ≥3 diagnoses relative to either alone. The randomized Canadian PRECISE trial included 453 biopsy-naïve patients with suspected cancer and PSA ≤20 ng/mL. MRI followed by targeted biopsy only for PI-RADS 3 or higher (MRI-TB) was noninferior to systematic TRUS biopsy for Grade Group 2 or greater cancer: 35% vs. 30%, respectively; absolute difference, 5%; 97.5% 1-sided CI, -3.4% to infinity; noninferiority margin, -5%. In the MRI-TB arm, 37% had negative MRI and avoided biopsy, and adverse events were less frequent. The report gives Grade Group 1 detection as 22% vs. 10% and a risk difference of -11.6% (95% CI, -18.2% to -4.9%), describing lower detection with MRI-TB. In the randomized population-based GÖTEBORG-2 trial, >37,000 people aged 50 to 60 years underwent regular PSA testing; those with PSA ≥3 ng/mL received MRI and were allocated 2:1 to MRI-targeted biopsy alone or targeted plus systematic biopsy. All 5994 reference-group patients were biopsied, whereas 262 of 11,986 experimental-group participants (of 268 with positive MRI) underwent targeted biopsy. Clinically insignificant cancer was diagnosed in 66 experimental-group participants (0.6%) and 72 reference-group participants (1.2%; 95% CI, −1.0 to −0.4; relative risk, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.33–0.64; P < .001). Clinically significant cancer occurred in 110 (0.9%) versus 68 (1.1%; relative risk, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.60–1.10). Systematic biopsy alone detected ten intermediate-risk, clinically significant cancers (0.2%). Omitting systematic cores therefore reduced insignificant diagnoses by approximately 50% but missed intermediate-risk cancer in approximately 0.2%; the low experimental-group biopsy rate prevents determining the true number missed, and the panel continues to recommend both methods. Other studies and a 2019 Cochrane review of 18 cross-sectional studies support better significant-cancer detection and less insignificant-cancer detection with MRI-based approaches, although individual studies have mixed findings. In one randomized study of 130 biopsy-naïve people, conventional biopsy and a pathway adding MRI and cognitive targeting had similar detection of any cancer (64% vs. 57%; P = .5) and significant cancer (55% vs. 45%; P = .8). Another randomized study of 212 biopsy-naïve patients detected more significant cancer with pre-biopsy MRI and conditional targeted fusion biopsy than with standard biopsy (43.9% vs. 18.1%; P < .001). Across studies, a PI-RADS ≤2 result might spare biopsy in 21% to 49% of biopsy-naïve people with elevated PSA, while missing clinically significant disease in 2% to 14% of study populations. A conventional systematic-biopsy pathway may miss a similar or greater proportion while detecting more indolent disease. Most MRI evidence originates in high-volume expert centers, and interpretation varies between readers; high-quality mpMRI and radiologic expertise are essential. The panel strongly recommends multiparametric MRI (category 1), if available, before image-guided biopsy. A negative MRI cannot rule out significant cancer: reported NPV is around 86% to 98%. Biopsy after a negative scan remains a consideration, particularly with high PSA density or concerning biomarkers. Image-guided biopsy should be routine. The preferred approach combines MRI-targeted and systematic sampling because systematic cores uniquely detect some high-grade cancers and support risk stratification, although some favor omitting them to reduce overdiagnosis. After at least one negative biopsy, high-quality MRI should be considered if not previously obtained because it may identify missed cancer.

document_sections.heading: Biomarker Testing
document_sections.content: PSA derivatives and other assays may improve specificity and reduce unnecessary biopsies. When biopsy criteria are met but the patient or clinician wants more precise risk assessment, biomarkers can help guide the decision, particularly at PSA 3 to 10 ng/mL; they have often been used after a negative biopsy. Their intended use is to reduce unnecessary sampling without missing many Grade group ≥2 cancers. The panel recommends considering tests validated in independent patient cohorts in peer-reviewed, multi-site studies. Validation across diverse populations differs, results can be difficult to interpret, specialist referral may be considered, and mpMRI is another option. The best way to combine biomarkers with MRI is uncertain. Direct comparisons have often been small and inconsistent, so the panel does not favor one biomarker over another. Testing may occur alone or alongside mpMRI and refined biopsy, but optimal sequencing and interpretation of discordant results remain unclear. Some recent studies suggest that an upfront biomarker followed by conditional MRI may efficiently assess persistently elevated PSA. Any results obtained should inform clinician–patient discussion about biopsy.

document_sections.heading: %fPSA
document_sections.content: Free PSA is the unbound fraction expressed relative to tPSA. It may assist early detection, staging, and monitoring. In most individuals, 60%–90% of circulating PSA is bound to endogenous protease inhibitors; the clinical significance of certain low-concentration complexes is unknown, and conventional assays cannot measure PSA bound to alpha-2-macroglobulin because its epitopes are shielded. Studies find significantly lower %fPSA in people with prostate cancer than in those without it. FDA approval covers early detection in individuals aged ≥50 years with a non-suspicious DRE and PSA between 4 and 10 ng/mL. In the supporting multi-institutional study, a 25% fPSA threshold detected 95% of cancers and avoided 20% of unnecessary biopsies. The guidelines offer %fPSA before an initial biopsy and after a negative biopsy.

document_sections.heading: PSA Density
document_sections.content: PSA density is PSA in ng/mL divided by image-measured prostate volume in cc. Lower density makes BPH more probable as an explanation for elevated PSA. Earlier studies proposed 0.15 ng/mL/g and reported avoidance of as many as 50% of unnecessary biopsies; subsequent work questioned that threshold's sensitivity. PSA density also correlates with cancer presence and aggressiveness and may predict adverse pathology and biochemical progression after treatment. The panel advises considering it when deciding on biopsy after negative mpMRI or in a biopsy-naïve patient with elevated PSA.

document_sections.heading: PCA3
document_sections.content: PCA3 is a prostate tissue-specific, noncoding RNA overexpressed in prostate cancer and measured in urine collected after DRE. Its principal potential use is repeat-biopsy assessment. In a prospective multicenter study of 466 people with at least one negative biopsy, a score threshold of 25 had sensitivity 78%, specificity 57%, NPV 90%, and PPV 34%; scores ≥25 were associated with 4.6 times the likelihood of a positive repeat biopsy compared with scores <25. An EDRN validation study enrolled 859 individuals at 11 centers. It reported PPV 80% (95% CI, 72%–86%) for initial biopsy and NPV 88% (95% CI, 81%–93%) for repeat biopsy. In the repeat setting, using PCA3 could avoid almost half of biopsies but miss high-grade disease in 3% with a low score; among previously unbiopsied people with a low score, high-grade disease risk was 13%. The panel therefore considers it inappropriate for initial-biopsy decisions. FDA approval permits its use with other factors when deciding whether people aged ≥50 years with one or more negative biopsies need another biopsy. It is a guideline option after biopsy.

document_sections.heading: PHI
document_sections.content: Prostate Health Index (PHI) combines tPSA, fPSA, and proPSA. A multicenter study in people with PSA 2 to 10 ng/mL found approximately twice the cancer-detection sensitivity of fPSA/tPSA and an AUC of 0.72 for distinguishing Grade Group ≥2 cancer from lower-grade cancer or a negative biopsy. Another prospective cohort reported AUC 0.815 for Grade Group ≥2 disease and proposed a score threshold of 24, potentially avoiding 36% of biopsies while missing approximately 2.5% of high-grade cancers. FDA approved PHI in 2012 for PSA 4 to 10 ng/mL. A clinical utility study in patients with normal DRE and PSA 4 to 10 ng/mL found fewer biopsies with PHI than in historical controls (36.4% vs. 60.3%; P < .0001); clinicians said PHI influenced decisions for 73%. High-grade cancers missed were not reported, and others estimated the proportion might reach 30%. PHI is an option before and after biopsy.

document_sections.heading: 4Kscore
document_sections.content: 4Kscore measures fPSA, tPSA, human kallikrein 2 (hK2), and intact PSA, and incorporates age, DRE, and prior biopsy status to estimate the percentage likelihood of Grade Group ≥2 cancer on biopsy. A prospective U.S. multi-institutional study of 1012 patients reported AUC 0.82. A biopsy threshold of ≥15% risk would have avoided 591 biopsies (58%), detected 183 high-grade tumors, and missed 48 (4.7% of the 1012 participants). Another prospective study of 6129 participants found AUC 0.82 (95% CI, 0.80–0.84); at a 6% high-grade risk threshold, 428 of 1000 could avoid biopsy while 119 of 133 high-grade cancers would be found and 14 of 133 missed. A multicenter utility study reported a 65% reduction in biopsies and an association between risk category and Gleason score (P < .01). A meta-analysis of 12 validation studies involving 11,134 patients calculated pooled AUC 0.81 (fixed effects 95% CI, 0.80–0.83) for Grade Group ≥2 cancer. By panel consensus, 4Kscore may be considered before biopsy or after a negative biopsy when clinically significant cancer remains a concern. No optimal threshold is established; patients and urologists should discuss results before deciding on biopsy.

document_sections.heading: ConfirmMDx
document_sections.content: ConfirmMDx is a tissue-based multiplex epigenetic test assessing promoter hypermethylation of GSTP1, APC, and RASSF1 in biopsy cores to refine repeat-biopsy decisions. It is run in one CLIA-certified laboratory and is not FDA approved. In the European MATLOC study, archived samples from 498 patients with negative biopsies and repeat sampling within 30 months produced NPV 90% (95% CI, 87%–93%); multivariable outcome prediction had OR, 3.17; 95% CI, 1.81–5.53. A U.S. validation study of 350 patients resampled within 24 months found NPV 88% (95% CI, 85%–91%) and multivariable OR, 2.69; 95% CI, 1.60–4.51. The panel considers ConfirmMDx an option when contemplating repeat biopsy because it may identify patients more likely to receive a cancer diagnosis. MolDX permits limited coverage to reduce unnecessary repeat biopsies.

document_sections.heading: ExoDx Prostate (IntelliScore)
document_sections.content: ExoDx Prostate (IntelliScore), or EPI, evaluates urinary exosome RNA expression of PCA3 and ERG, normalized to SPDEF, to distinguish Grade Group ≥2 cancer from Grade Group 1 or benign findings at initial biopsy. Its intended-use population includes previously unbiopsied patients >50 years with PSA 2 to 10 ng/mL. In a McKiernan et al study, AUC was 0.74 in training and 0.71 in validation; applying the training threshold to validation avoided 27% of biopsies (138 of 519) while missing 8% (12 of 148) of Grade Group ≥2 cancers. The algorithm was tested in 255 patients and an extended validation cohort of 519. Most exclusions reflected urine volume >49 mL, assay failure, or use outside the intended population. A separate 2-phase adaptive study enrolled 503 biopsy-naïve patients with PSA 2 to 10 ng/mL. Its first phase found AUC 0.70; at the validated 15.6 threshold, NPV was 89%, biopsies fell by 20%, and 7% of Grade Group ≥2 cancers were missed. Its second phase had not yet been reported. In a utility trial, 1094 patients cared for by 72 urologists in 24 practices were randomized to receive EPI results before biopsy or not. Results influenced biopsy decisions; the EPI arm diagnosed 30% more high-grade cancers, and investigators estimated 49% fewer missed high-grade cancers than in the control arm. The panel considers EPI an option before initial or repeat biopsy.

document_sections.heading: SelectMDx
document_sections.content: SelectMDx measures DLX1 and HOXC6 expression relative to KLK3 in urine after DRE. DLX1 and HOXC6 have been linked to cancer aggressiveness; the assay seeks to improve pre-biopsy detection of clinically significant disease while reducing unnecessary biopsies. Development used 519 patients and validation used 386 from two prospective multicenter studies. Gene expression alone predicted Grade Group ≥2 cancer with AUC 0.76, sensitivity 91%, specificity 36%, NPV 94%, and PPV 27%. A model adding PSA, PSA density, DRE, previous negative biopsies, age, and family history yielded AUC 0.90 in training and 0.86 (95% CI, 0.80–0.92) in validation. A retrospective study of 172 patients compared SelectMDx with MRI findings: AUC for predicting MRI outcome was 0.83 for SelectMDx, versus 0.66 for PSA and 0.65 for PCA2. A further multicenter study used urine from 1955 people; in its 916-patient validation cohort, detection of Grade Group >2 cancer had AUC 0.85, sensitivity 93%, specificity 47%, and NPV 95%. Restricting analysis to PSA <10 ng/mL gave 0.82, 89%, 53%, and 95%, respectively. The panel considers SelectMDx potentially informative and an option in previously unbiopsied patients.

document_sections.heading: IsoPSA
document_sections.content: IsoPSA uses a blood-based aqueous 2-phase process to separate and detect PSA isoforms. A prospective multicenter validation in 888 patients scheduled for biopsy found AUC 0.783 (95% CI, 0.752–0.814) for Grade Group ≥2 cancer, sensitivity 90.2% (95% CI, 86.4–93.0), specificity 45.5% (95% CI, 41.4–49.6), PPV 47.7% (95% CI, 45.7–49.8), and NPV 89.3 (95% CI, 85.6–92.2). In a real-world study (n = 900), 38 clinicians changed biopsy and/or MRI recommendations for 66% of patients after receiving results, with a net 55% decrease in biopsy recommendations. The panel considers IsoPSA before biopsy and after a negative biopsy when clinically significant cancer remains a concern.

document_sections.heading: MyProstateScore
document_sections.content: MyProstateScore (MPS) combines serum total PSA with post-DRE urinary PCA3 and TMPRSS2:ERG expression. ERG rearrangements occur in approximately half of prostate cancers; the TMPRSS2:ERG fusion is frequent and appears early in disease development. Early studies suggested that combining markers improved prediction of biopsy findings. In a validation cohort of 1244 people scheduled for biopsy, 80% had no prior biopsy. For any cancer, AUC was 0.751 with MPS versus 0.585 with PSA alone; for Grade Group ≥2 cancer, AUC was 0.772 versus 0.651. Another validation cohort included 1525 initial-biopsy referrals and reported sensitivity 97% and NPV 98% for Grade Group ≥2 disease. Its authors calculated that testing could avoid 33% of unnecessary biopsies while missing 3% of Grade Group ≥2 cancers. The panel considers MPS before biopsy and after a negative biopsy when significant cancer remains a concern.

document_sections.heading: Additional Biomarker Tests
document_sections.content: For additional assays discussed below, longer cohort follow-up is needed to determine whether missed cancers are subsequently detected, and validation in other cohorts is needed before accepting them as alternatives or preferable tests. Because independent validation, performance in other screened populations, incremental value, and cost-effectiveness remain uncertain, the panel cannot recommend routine use at present. A single negative biopsy can miss cancers at rates as high as 25%, and pathologic review of surgical specimens upgrades 32%–49% of cancers initially classified Grade Group 1 on biopsy.

document_sections.heading: MiR Sentinel Prostate Cancer Test
document_sections.content: MiR Sentinel Prostate Cancer Test examines small noncoding RNAs from urinary exosomes to distinguish prostate cancer from no evidence of cancer. Wang and colleagues developed it in 235 participants and validated it in a case-control sample of 1436 people spanning a wide range of PSA values. Sensitivity and specificity for high-grade cancer (Grade Group 2 or higher) were described as very high. Further validation is needed, especially for people with negative DRE and PSA 2.5–10.0 ng/mL.

document_sections.heading: Stockholm3
document_sections.content: Stockholm3 combines age, first-degree family history, prior biopsy, PSA, fPSA, %fPSA, hK2, MIC1, MSMB, a genetic score based on 254 SNPs, a separate HOXB13 SNP variable, prostate volume, and DRE. In Swedish patients with PSA ≥3 ng/mL, it reduced biopsies by 34% relative to PSA alone with similar sensitivity. In the prospective randomized open-label noninferiority STHLM3-MRI trial, 2293 Swedish participants with PSA ≥3 ng/mL or Stockholm3 above a specified threshold were assigned 2:3 to systematic biopsy or biparametric MRI followed by targeted and systematic biopsy after a positive scan. AUC for Grade Group ≥2 cancer was 0.76 (95% CI, 0.72–0.80) for Stockholm3 and 0.60 (95% CI, 0.54–0.65) for PSA. The Stockholm3-plus-MRI pathway detected more Grade Group ≥2 cancers and fewer low-grade cancers and required fewer biopsies than PSA followed by systematic biopsy.

document_sections.heading: Biopsy Technique
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses image-guided initial biopsy, MRI-targeted sampling, and assessment after a negative biopsy. Its preferred strategy uses targeting when available while retaining systematic sampling where indicated; transrectal and transperineal access are both considered reasonable.

document_sections.heading: Initial Biopsy
document_sections.content: The recommended initial procedure is image-guided biopsy, preferably targeting lesions identified on pre-biopsy MRI, although biopsy without targeting is an option. If systematic sampling is performed, the panel recommends an extended pattern of at least 12 cores covering medial and lateral peripheral sextant sites and suspicious lesions; this detects more cancer than sextant schemes. Routine anterior sampling is unsupported, but it may be added at repeat biopsy for persistently elevated PSA. Image-guided sampling can use transrectal or transperineal access. PROMIS found greater significant-cancer detection with transperineal template biopsy than transrectal biopsy. Evidence that transperineal biopsy reduces sepsis and antibiotic need is conflicting; extensive perineal templates may increase urinary retention. No definitive comparison of limited transperineal with conventional transrectal biopsy has been conducted. The panel considers both access routes reasonable.

document_sections.heading: Targeted Biopsy Techniques
document_sections.content: Targeting methods include visual or cognitive ultrasound targeting based on MRI, TRUS-MRI fusion of stored and live images, and direct in-bore MR-guided sampling. MRI followed by lesion targeting improves detection of higher-risk Grade Group ≥3 disease while reducing detection of Grade Group 1 disease; available data suggest similar significant-cancer detection across targeting methods. Evidence supporting MRI and targeting at initial biopsy is increasingly compelling, but combining targeted and systematic cores usually improves significant-cancer yield and sensitivity. The combined approach is preferred when MRI targeting is available, at least for initial biopsy.

document_sections.heading: Repeat Biopsies
document_sections.content: A negative biopsy does not rule out cancer on later sampling. When suspicion persists, multiparametric MRI followed by an appropriate targeted method may be considered, as may biomarker testing to guide a repeat-biopsy decision.

document_sections.heading: Targeted Biopsy for Repeat Biopsy
document_sections.content: In a study in which patients with abnormal MRI proceeded to MRI-TRUS fusion targeting, targeted cores detected significantly more cancer than systematic cores (30% vs. 8.2%); about 12% without MRI-suspicious lesions had intermediate-risk tumors, and overall detection among people with prior negative biopsies was 51%. After one or more negative image-guided biopsies, MRI with targeted biopsy can be considered for patients at high risk, such as those with persistently elevated or rising PSA. Reported detection after previous negative biopsy ranges from 34% to 51% with fusion targeting and 41% to 56% with direct MR guidance. A prospective study of 583 patients, 56% of whom had a prior negative biopsy, used MRI and systematic 12-core biopsy, with fusion targeting for visible lesions; a higher MRI suspicion score increased the likelihood of Grade Group ≥2 cancer by 3.3-fold (95% CI, 2.2–5.1; P < .0001). A meta-analysis of 16 studies involving 1926 people found improved significant-cancer detection with MRI targeting versus standard TRUS biopsy after a negative result. High-resolution micro-US performed similarly to mpMRI for cancer detection in another comparison. In a retrospective cohort of 105 patients with elevated PSA and prior negative biopsy, MRI was followed by systematic 12-core and fusion-targeted sampling regardless of MRI results. Cancer was found in 36 (34%); 21 of 23 cancers (91%) found by targeting met the study's significance definition of Grade Group 2 or mean core length ≥4 mm, versus 15 of 28 (54%) found systematically. Targeting missed significant cancer in two patients versus five with standard biopsy. The panel advises strongly considering targeted methods when a previous biopsy was negative but PSA or biomarker findings sustain concern.

document_sections.heading: Saturation Biopsy Techniques
document_sections.content: Saturation biopsy samples the prostate systematically every few millimeters to improve detection relative to standard 12-core sampling. In a transperineal mapping study of 436 patients, biopsy density greater than 1.5 was associated with a 1.5-fold higher cancer diagnosis rate and greater detection of higher-volume Grade Group 1 disease. The panel does not recommend saturation biopsy for everyone with a prior negative biopsy, given the benefits of MRI and targeted biopsy. Transrectal and transperineal saturation appear to detect cancer at similar rates; a direct repeat-biopsy comparison found 31.4% versus 25.7% (P = .3). Transperineal access may reduce infection, sample the gland more thoroughly, improve acceptability, and improve assessment of volume and grade, but may increase urinary retention and often needs more extensive anesthesia. Some studies reported zero or near-zero sepsis with this approach. Transrectal biopsy can routinely be performed in an office. A transperineal template-mapping study reported cancer detection of 55.5%, 41.7%, and 34.4% after 1, 2, and ≥3 previous negative biopsies, respectively. In a prospective nonrandomized study after one negative biopsy, transrectal saturation found more cancer than extended 12–14-core biopsy (32.7% vs. 24.9%; P = .0075); insignificant-cancer detection did not differ significantly (40.1% vs. 32.6%; P = .2).

document_sections.heading: Risks of Biopsy
document_sections.content: Biopsy can cause infections, particularly with antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli, including UTI, epididymitis, orchitis, prostatitis, and sepsis. In U.S. hospitals from 2009 to 2016, 30-day invasive Escherichia coli infection risk was 5.0 per 1000 patients. Antimicrobial prophylaxis is generally used for transrectal biopsy to prevent infection and subsequent antibiotic use. Reports indicate resistance to fluoroquinolone in up to 78% of post-biopsy infections, frequently alongside resistance to other agents. FDA warnings for fluoroquinolones include potentially permanent tendon, muscle, joint, nerve, and central nervous system effects, aortic rupture or tear, serious hypoglycemia, and mental-health effects. The AUA considers fluoroquinolone prophylaxis appropriate in some centers or circumstances and lists 1st/2nd generation cephalosporin with or without aminoglycoside, or 3rd generation cephalosporin, as other options. Measures proposed to limit resistant infections include stringent biopsy selection, transperineal biopsy, culture-directed prophylaxis after pre-biopsy rectal sampling, and selectively adding a second antibiotic for patients at elevated infection risk. Evidence on lower sepsis and antibiotic need with transperineal access is conflicting. In randomized ProBEPC, infectious and noninfectious outcomes did not differ statistically between transrectal (n = 351) and transperineal (n = 367) biopsy, supporting both as reasonable. Other potential effects include rectal bleeding, hematuria, vasovagal events, fever, hematospermia, and dysuria; up to 90% report procedural discomfort. Topical lidocaine gel and injectable nerve block safely reduce discomfort: topical treatment better addresses probe insertion, whereas periprostatic injection better addresses sampling pain. Small trials suggest benefit from combining lidocaine suppository with periprostatic block or lidocaine with pelvic plexus block. In a randomized trial of 216 patients receiving TRUS-guided transperineal biopsy, periprostatic block plus subcutaneous perineal anesthesia and intrarectal lidocaine gel produced less biopsy pain, shorter procedures (P < .05), more stable hemodynamic and respiratory measures, and fewer surgical complications (P < .05) than total intravenous anesthesia. Minor anesthetic measures should be considered for all patients, especially with extended or saturation sampling. Deep sedation or general anesthesia may help those with anal strictures, poor tolerance of local anesthesia, or inadequate periprostatic block.

document_sections.heading: Summary of NCCN Recommendations for Early Detection
document_sections.content: The guideline summarizes a risk-adapted, preference-sensitive early detection program, with counseling and assessment before testing, repeat intervals guided by PSA and risk, and imaging and selective biomarkers to guide biopsy.

document_sections.heading: General Considerations
document_sections.content: Early detection decisions require consideration of age, life expectancy, family history, African ancestry, inherited mutations, previous tests, general health, comorbidity, and patient preferences, alongside discussion of benefits and harms. Guidance does not replace a clinician's full history and examination. Early prostate cancer has no identifiable symptoms; advanced disease can cause urinary obstruction, prostatic bleeding, hematospermia, or bone pain. Symptoms from benign prostatic enlargement should be distinguished during counseling. Prior DRE, PSA, PSA derivatives, and biopsy results should be reviewed. Patients should understand that detection seeks aggressive cancers but also finds low-risk disease that may be managed with active surveillance rather than immediate treatment. The panel recommends offering baseline PSA to healthy, informed people at average risk aged 45 to 75 years and to those with African ancestry, risk-associated germline mutations, and/or suspicious family history at ages 40 to 75 years. Baseline DRE may complement PSA; elevated PSA should be confirmed. For average-risk people <75 years with PSA below 1 ng/mL, recommended repeat testing is every 2 to 4 years; at PSA 1 to 3 ng/mL, every 1 to 2 years. With elevated risk and PSA ≤3 ng/mL, the interval is 1 to 2 years. The panel strongly recommends multiparametric MRI before biopsy when available. For PSA >3 ng/mL when greater specificity is desired, %fPSA, 4Kscore, SelectMDx, ExoDx Prostate, PHI, MPS, and IsoPSA may be considered before biopsy. After a negative biopsy with persistent higher risk, options include PHI, %fPSA, 4Kscore, ConfirmMDx, PCA3, MPS, and IsoPSA. Biopsy decisions should not rely on PSA threshold alone; age, family history, PSA kinetics, ancestry, health, preferences, MRI, and biomarkers also matter. High suspicion of clinically significant cancer warrants image-guided transrectal or transperineal biopsy; routine MRI targeting is recommended where available. PSA testing after age >75 years warrants cautious consideration only in very healthy patients (category 2B), with careful biopsy assessment. Panel members uniformly discourage testing those unlikely to benefit because of age or comorbidity. The panel considers these early detection recommendations linked to the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer.

document_sections.heading: Management of Biopsy Results
document_sections.content: Management depends on whether biopsy shows cancer, intraductal findings, atypia, high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia, or a benign result. A negative biopsy cannot definitively exclude cancer, so follow-up is adapted to the finding, prior MRI quality, and ongoing clinical suspicion.

document_sections.heading: Cancer
document_sections.content: Biopsy-confirmed prostate cancer should receive comprehensive care according to the NCCN Guidelines for Prostate Cancer. Routine repeat biopsy is not recommended after a cancer diagnosis, except in particular situations, including suspicion of more aggressive disease than initially sampled or assessment of a patient otherwise eligible for active surveillance under the treatment guideline.

document_sections.heading: Intraductal Carcinoma Without Invasive Cancer
document_sections.content: Intraductal carcinoma (IDC) is an independent adverse pathological factor in prostatectomy and needle-biopsy specimens and may affect response to current advanced-cancer regimens. In prostatectomy specimens, IDC accompanies higher Gleason score, larger tumors, more extraprostatic extension, seminal vesicle invasion, and pelvic nodal metastasis; it independently predicts biochemical recurrence, progression-free survival, and cancer-specific mortality. In biopsy material, it usually accompanies high-grade, high-volume disease and predicts adverse prostatectomy findings and poor outcomes, including early biochemical recurrence, cancer-specific survival, survival with distant metastasis at presentation, and metastasis after radiation for intermediate- or high-risk cancer. It may resist existing aggressive-cancer regimens and require multimodal or novel treatment. IDC on biopsy strongly suggests high-grade cancer. When IDC occurs without identified invasive carcinoma, the guideline recommends proceeding directly to definitive therapy; otherwise, careful evaluation with strong consideration of MRI-targeted repeat biopsy to seek invasive cancer is indicated.

document_sections.heading: Atypical Intraductal Proliferation Without Invasive Cancer
document_sections.content: Atypical intraductal proliferation (AIP) denotes intraductal changes more architecturally complex and/or cytologically atypical than typical HGPIN but insufficient for IDC. On needle biopsy it may mark unsampled cancer and is associated with a 50% increased risk of invasive carcinoma and/or IDC at repeat biopsy. One study found worse pathological features in cancers associated with AIP than in those associated with HGPIN; another found similarities between AIP-associated and IDC-associated carcinoma. If AIP appears without invasive carcinoma, repeat biopsy combining MRI targeting and systematic sampling is recommended to look for invasion.

document_sections.heading: Other Notable Pathologic Features and Benign Results
document_sections.content: Most biopsy findings are benign, but a negative result cannot exclude cancer. Patients with benign findings, HGPIN, or atypia suspicious for cancer need follow-up that balances significant-cancer detection against excess testing and overdiagnosis. Studies report Grade Group ≥2 cancer on repeat biopsy in 4% to 9% of patients after ASAP, HGPIN, or benign findings, without significant differences between those groups; Grade Group 1 detection is 24% to 30%. In a Danish study after an initially negative biopsy, 15-year prostate cancer-specific mortality was 1.3% with PSA <10 ng/mL and 4.6% with PSA >20 ng/mL. Approximately 10% of biopsied patients have HGPIN. Its nuclei resemble malignant cells, but an acinar basal layer distinguishes it from cancer. After HGPIN, repeat-biopsy cancer detection was approximately 50% with historical sextant sampling, versus approximately 10% to 20% and occasionally higher with contemporary extended sampling; most detected cancers are low grade. Atypia, also termed atypical small acinar proliferation (ASAP), describes glands resembling adenocarcinoma without meeting full malignant criteria. Unlike HGPIN, ASAP is not a distinct pathological diagnosis and may reflect a benign mimic or insufficiently definitive cancer. Approximately 5% of patients receive an atypia result. Even after extended initial sampling, repeat biopsy detects cancer in 50% or more, usually in the initially atypical region. For benign results, suspicious atypia, or HGPIN with a prior high-quality mpMRI, PSA and DRE are recommended at 12- to 24-month intervals, and certain biomarkers may be considered. Without prior high-quality mpMRI, biomarkers and/or mpMRI should be considered. With atypia, consider repeat biopsy in 12–24 months with relatively greater sampling of the atypical site. For any of these findings, high cancer suspicion warrants repeat biopsy using refined techniques. Positive mpMRI, persistently high PSA, shorter PSA doubling time, high PSA density, and/or abnormal DRE heighten concern.

document_sections.heading: Summary
document_sections.content: The guideline describes systematic, evidence-based use of PSA variants and other techniques to improve early cancer detection while limiting unnecessary biopsies. It is intended for people who choose early detection, not as an argument for population-wide screening. Decisions on treatment after diagnosis lie outside its scope. The panel plans to review newly validated modalities annually and revise its algorithms as evidence develops, potentially incorporating investigational serum markers. The algorithms aim to help patients and clinicians choose an early detection approach and decide whether biopsy is needed; clinicians should apply independent judgment to individual circumstances.
